clause_name: Section 2 — Term and Exercise of Option
issue: "Shall continue in effect for a period of not less than one (1) year" sets a floor but no outside date, so "its expiration" has no ascertainable meaning and the Option's duration is genuinely open.
court_defect: The court construed whether the word “may” made the prescribed notice requirements optional, concluding instead that it referred to GSA’s discretion to exercise the option within the specified time frame.
evidence: Plaintiff argues that Paragraph 2 of the Option Agreement, which defines the required method of notice, is merely an "optional" or "preferred choice” due to the use of the word "may." Pl.’s Resp. 7. The Court finds this argument without merit, as the contract terms plainly and unambiguously allude to the GSA's ability to exercise the option at its will within the specified time frame, and do not render the notice requirements themselves optional.
reason: The proposed issue concerns whether “not less than one (1) year” fails to establish an ascertainable expiration date. The court instead construed “may” and whether the notice method was optional; its reference to a “specified time frame” does not show that it considered the alleged lack of an outside date.

issue: The passive-conduit acknowledgment cannot be squared with the very next paragraph of Section 13, which reserves the right 'to review and delete any Content that, in its sole judgment, violates' the Agreement, with Section 11's removal of reviews on resolution, and with Section 20's control over retention of ratings. The instrument describes Angie's List as both a passive carrier and an active editor of the Content.
court_defect: The court construed the “passive conduit” language, together with Sections 1 and 14, as a representation that consumer reviews and ratings would be unshaped by outside input. It held that alleged paid alteration of ratings and suppression of negative reviews plausibly breached that representation.
evidence: These provisions unambiguously depict the website with which Moore contracted as a provider rating system based on “firsthand” consumer reviews, unshaped by input from any other source. She alleges a breach by averring that (1) an electrician of her acquaintance disclosed that he pays Angie’s List to alter his rating, and (2) she could not initially view all negative reviews of the provider she contracted with — both of which counter Angie’s List’s representation that it is simply a passive conduit for the publication of content about providers.
reason: Both the proposed issue and the passage concern the tension between being a “passive conduit” and actively shaping ratings or reviews. But the proposed issue alleges an internal conflict with Sections 11, 13, and 20, whereas the court addressed whether Angie’s List’s alleged conduct breached the passive-conduit representation and did not construe the cited editorial-control clauses.

issue: Read against Section 1's description of the service and Section 13's passive-conduit and no-liability language, it is unclear whether Section 14 disclaims responsibility for Angie's List's own conduct in compiling and presenting ratings and advertising, or only for the Service Providers' conduct. The instrument as a whole does not settle which.
court_defect: The court construed Section 14 together with Sections 1 and 13 as representing that Angie’s List was a passive, consumer-based rating system whose rankings and reviews were not shaped by paid or other outside input. It treated Angie’s List’s alleged alteration of ratings and suppression of reviews as potentially breaching all three provisions, without separately parsing Section 14’s no-liability language.
evidence: These provisions unambiguously depict the website with which Moore contracted as a provider rating system based on “firsthand” consumer reviews, unshaped by input from any other source. She alleges a breach by averring that (1) an electrician of her acquaintance disclosed that he pays Angie’s List to alter his rating, and (2) she could not initially view all negative reviews of the provider she contracted with — both of which counter Angie’s List’s representation that it is simply a passive conduit for the publication of content about providers. Again, taking her allegations as true (and disregarding the defendant’s factual aver-ments, as we must), these allegations suffice to nudge Moore’s claim as to those three provisions alone over the crucial line that separates conceivable and plausible, see Twombly, 550 U.S. at 570, 127 S.Ct. 1955.
reason: The proposed issue and the court both address how Section 14 operates alongside Sections 1 and 13 when Angie’s List itself allegedly manipulates ratings or presentation. The alignment is not exact because the court treated the provisions collectively as affirmative representations and did not expressly analyze whether Section 14’s responsibility disclaimer reaches Angie’s List’s own conduct rather than only Service Provider conduct.

issue: The whole formula runs off "the value of Covered Property at the time of loss", and the form never says whether that value is actual cash value or replacement cost — the choice that decides whether any coinsurance penalty exists at all.
court_defect: The court construed the undefined term “value” in the coinsurance formula, holding that it means replacement cost when the insured elects replacement-cost coverage. It also addressed which costs are included in that replacement-cost valuation.
evidence: The coinsurance provision states that State Auto will not pay the full amount of loss if the “value” of “Covered Property” shows that it is underinsured. “Value” means “replacement cost,” as defined in Section G.3, as held in the Missouri litigation.
reason: The proposed issue identifies uncertainty over whether “value” means actual cash value or replacement cost. The passage expressly construes that same term in the same coinsurance formula and holds that it means replacement cost; the lack of an express discussion of actual cash value is only a minor difference.

issue: The Replacement Cost paragraph is spliced together with Agreed Value text, so the operative sentence — that "Replacement Cost (without deduction for depreciation) replaces Actual Cash Value in the Loss Condition, Valuation" — is separated from its own opening words and its reach is not readable as printed.
court_defect: The court construed whether “replacement cost” under Section G includes law-and-ordinance compliance costs after the relevant exclusion was excised, considering the separate Additional Coverages provision. It did not address any mechanical splicing or unreadable sentence in Section G.3(a).
evidence: Therefore, the Court finds that even without the exclusion found in G.3.f, the calculation of replacement cost for purposes of determining the coinsurance percentage does not include law and ordinance costs.
reason: The proposed issue concerns a printing or assembly error that separates the operative words of the Replacement Cost paragraph. The passage instead construes the substantive scope of “replacement cost” after removal of G.3.f and its interaction with law-and-ordinance coverage, giving no sign that the court engaged with the alleged splice.

clause_name: Section A.1 — Actual Loss of Business Income
issue: The promise is to pay "the actual loss of Business Income you sustain due to the necessary 'suspension' of your 'operations' during the 'period of restoration'", and both "actual loss ... you sustain" and "necessary" suspension are left undefined as measures of recovery.
court_defect: The court construed what constitutes an “actual loss” of business income—specifically, whether income earned by investing the insurer’s advance payment must be deducted from recovery. It did not construe the meaning of a “necessary” suspension.
evidence: The Court agrees that the Policy language allowing Boardwalk to recover for “actual loss” of “business income” means that it must back out from the loss any interest income Boardwalk earned during the period of restoration that was available to pay Boardwalk’s expenses.
reason: The proposed issue identifies “actual loss ... you sustain” as unclear as a measure of recovery, and the court directly determined how that phrase affects the recovery calculation. Alignment is partial because the proposal also challenges “necessary” suspension, which the passage does not construe.

clause_name: Section C.3(a) — Business Income Loss Determination
issue: The measure rests on "[t]he likely Net Income of the business if no physical loss or damage had occurred" and on operating expenses "necessary to resume 'operations' with the same quality of service", neither of which is defined or given a method of proof.
court_defect: The court construed the meaning of “necessary to resume operations,” specifically whether saved depreciation qualifies as a noncontinuing operating expense deductible from rental-value business income benefits.
evidence: The Policy provides that loss is determined based on “[t]he operating expenses, including payroll expenses, necessary to resume ‘operations’ with the same quality of service that existed just before the direct physical loss or damage.” The parties dispute the meaning of “necessary to resume operations.”
reason: The proposed issue expressly identifies the undefined meaning of expenses “necessary to resume ‘operations’ with the same quality of service,” and the court directly resolved a dispute over that phrase’s meaning. The alignment is not complete because the proposal also challenges the separate “likely Net Income” language and lack of a proof method, neither of which the passage addresses.

clause_name: Section F.3 — Period of Restoration Definition
issue: The period ends on "[t]he date when the property at the described premises should be repaired, rebuilt or replaced with reasonable speed and similar quality" — a hypothetical date fixed by "should" and "reasonable speed", neither of which the policy defines or benchmarks.
court_defect: The court construed how the phrase “should be ... replaced with reasonable speed and similar quality” determines the restoration period’s endpoint, including whether that endpoint is theoretical rather than the actual reconstruction date. It also found a factual dispute over what constituted “reasonable speed.”
evidence: The parties dispute when the period of restoration ends. The issue turns on the meaning of the Policy language “when the property ... should be ... replaced with reasonable speed and similar quality.” Courts construing similar policy language conclude that it refers to the theoretical time period it takes to resume business.
reason: The proposed issue identifies the same language and argues that “should” and “reasonable speed” establish an unbenchmarked hypothetical endpoint. The court expressly interpreted that language as creating a theoretical restoration period, although it did not expressly characterize the problem as a lack of policy definitions or benchmarks.

issue: The integration clause sweeps in "the other agreements and instruments executed and delivered in connection with the issuance of the Series 2004 Auction Bonds" without identifying them, so the boundary of the integrated whole is undefined. "Relating to the subject matter hereof" carries the same open edge.
court_defect: The passage shows a dispute over the merger clause’s scope—particularly whether “instruments executed and delivered” encompasses other written agreements concerning the 2004 issuance and how “the subject matter hereof” limits that scope.
evidence: Goldman Sachs countered, however, that the merger clause’s language — stipulating that it covered “instruments executed and delivered” — indicates that it covered more than just any potential oral agreements that may have existed, and-“obyiously ... [included] other written, agreements that deal with the 2004 issuance.” Tr. .at 70:5-14 (Schwartz).
reason: The proposed issue and the passage both concern which other agreements fall within the integrated whole and thus address the same underlying scope problem. The passage construes that language as including written agreements dealing with the 2004 issuance, but it does not expressly focus on the drafting omission identified by the proposal—the failure to identify those agreements—or declare the boundary undefined.

issue: The clause designates "the United States District Court in the County of New York", a court that does not exist — New York County lies in the Southern District — so whether it names a federal court, state courts in that county, or is unenforceable is genuinely open. It also does not say in terms that the chosen forum is exclusive despite "shall be brought".
court_defect: The court construes the scope of “arising out of,” deciding that it requires origin and a causal connection and that the asserted claims fall within that scope. It does not construe whether the named court exists or whether “shall be brought” makes the forum exclusive.
evidence: The Court interprets “arising out of’ a contract to mean originating from, and bearing causal connection with, the contract.
reason: The proposed issue concerns the forum’s defective designation and the clause’s asserted silence about exclusivity. The quoted passage instead interprets the distinct phrase “arising out of” to determine which claims are covered, so it addresses a different defect in the same provision.

issue: Endorsement 15 (Service of Suit) provides that 'If the insured requests, the company will submit to the jurisdiction of any court of competent jurisdiction' and will accept that court's final decision, which cannot be squared with exclusive New York jurisdiction. The instrument gives the insured a choice of forum in one place and denies it in another.
court_defect: The court construed the apparent conflict between the Policy’s exclusive-New-York forum-selection clause and the Service of Suit Endorsement allowing the insured to choose any court of competent jurisdiction. It resolved that conflict by holding that the Endorsement amended and supplanted the forum-selection clause.
evidence: The Endorsement, when read in isolation, seems to conflict with the forum-selection clause because the nearly identical language used in both provisions leads to opposite results: one mandates New, York as the exclusive jurisdiction, while the other states the company will submit to the jurisdiction of any competent court and accept its final decision.
reason: The proposed issue identifies exactly the conflict the court addressed: one provision requires exclusive New York jurisdiction, while Endorsement 15 permits the insured to select any competent court. Although the court ultimately reconciled the provisions by treating the Endorsement as an amendment, it expressly construed the same alleged incompatibility.

issue: The company's promise to 'submit to the jurisdiction of any court of competent jurisdiction' at the insured's request cannot be reconciled with General Condition IX.I., which makes New York jurisdiction 'exclusive'. Whether the service of suit endorsement waives or merely supplements the forum clause is the classic dispute over this pairing.
court_defect: The court construed whether Endorsement 15’s promise to submit to any competent court conflicts with and amends or supplants the policy’s exclusive New York forum-selection clause, or instead merely provides personal jurisdiction without affecting that clause.
evidence: The parties provide two possible interpretations of the interplay between the forum-selection clause and the Endorsement. Rembrandt’s interpretation is that the Endorsement is meant as an amendment and thereby changes the Policy’s general jurisdiction and venue terms. (PI. Resp. at 1.) Illinois Union posits that the Endorsement merely conveys personal jurisdiction over it and has no impact on the forum-selection clause. (Def. Reply at 1.)
reason: The proposed issue identifies the exact conflict and interpretive choice the court addressed: whether the endorsement overrides the exclusive New York clause or merely supplements it by conveying personal jurisdiction. The court ultimately held that the endorsement amends and supplants the forum-selection clause.

issue: The promise to 'accept the final decision of that court' reinforces the insured's forum choice under the Service of Suit endorsement and pulls against the exclusive New York jurisdiction required by General Condition IX.I. Read with the preceding sentence it is the strongest textual answer to that clause.
court_defect: The court construed the apparent conflict between the Endorsement’s promise to submit to any competent court and accept its final decision and the Policy’s clause requiring exclusive New York jurisdiction. It resolved that conflict by holding that the Endorsement amended and supplanted the forum-selection clause.
evidence: However, the Endorsement, using similar language, reads “if the insured requests, the company will' submit to the jurisdiction of any court of competent jurisdiction ,.. and will accept the final decision of that court.” (Id.) The Endorsement, when read in isolation, seems to conflict with the forum-selection clause because the nearly identical language used in both provisions leads to opposite results: one mandates New, York as the exclusive jurisdiction, while the other states the company will submit to the jurisdiction of any competent court and accept its final decision.
reason: The proposed issue identifies the acceptance-of-decision promise, read with the preceding submission language, as supporting the insured’s forum choice against exclusive New York jurisdiction. The court expressly analyzed that same language, the same conflict, and concluded that the Endorsement supplanted the New York forum-selection clause.

issue: The saving clause preserves the Policy's terms 'OTHER THAN AS ABOVE STATED', so whether the preceding submission to 'any court of competent jurisdiction' is one of the things 'above stated' that does vary General Condition IX.I. is precisely what the sentence leaves open. It is the pivot on which the forum dispute turns.
court_defect: The court construed whether the saving clause’s “OTHER THAN AS ABOVE STATED” exception allows the Service of Suit Endorsement to amend and supplant the Policy’s forum-selection clause. It held that, read as a whole, the Endorsement unambiguously gives the insured the choice of any competent court.
evidence: The Endorsement ends by stating: “NOTHING HEREIN CONTAINED SHALL BE HELD TO VARY, ALTER, WAIVE OR EXTEND ANY OF THE TERMS, CONDITIONS, OR LIMITATIONS OF THE POLICY TO WHIGH THIS ENDORSEMENT IS ATTACHED OTHER THAN AS ABOVE STATED.” (Id.) (emphasis added). Accordingly, this Court concludes that the plain meaning of this language is quite clear — the Endorsement changes the Policy with respect to the contents of the Endorsément, which indicates that the insured may choose. any competent court in which to sue the insurer.
reason: The proposed issue identifies whether “OTHER THAN AS ABOVE STATED” makes the preceding competent-court language an amendment to the Policy’s forum-selection condition. That is the exact interpretive question the court resolved, although the court rejected the proposal’s suggestion that the sentence leaves the matter open and instead found the amendment unambiguous.

issue: The promise of $60,300 is made "subject to the terms and conditions of this Agreement, including any applicable adjustment, forfeiture and adjusted time of payment provisions," a catch-all that does not identify which provisions those are. Its reach against the specific forfeiture triggers in Section 2(c) and Section 14 is open to argument.
court_defect: The court construed the $60,300 payment as conditional on Ryder remaining employed through the Retention Period and as forfeitable if Shell concluded that she failed to meet performance expectations. The litigated question was whether alleged FMLA protection prevented Shell from relying on her absences to terminate her and deny payment, not whether the catch-all failed to identify the applicable forfeiture provisions.
evidence: . Ryder does not argue that the Retention Agreement is ambiguous, but rather that she is entitled to receive payment under the Retention Agreement because she is entitled .to FMLA, protection for the absences alleged and, as such, Shell is precluded from relying on those absences in terminating .her employment and denying her the retention payment. This Court does not agree.
reason: The passage addresses the relationship between the payment promise and the agreement’s employment and forfeiture conditions, so it is related to the proposed issue’s concern about the reach of forfeiture provisions. But it expressly says Ryder did not assert ambiguity and does not construe any uncertainty about which provisions the catch-all incorporates, making the specific defect different.

clause_name: General subsection b — At-will employment and payment effect
issue: "The Payment may be affected by a change in your duties or position as set forth below" is indeterminate about whether "affected" means only the proration in Section 2(a) or something broader. The permissive "may" leaves the consequence of a position change unfixed.
court_defect: The passage does not show the court construing any ambiguity in subsection b’s phrase “The Payment may be affected.” It instead addresses Ryder’s theory that FMLA protection prevented Shell from terminating her and denying the payment, then relies on separate continued-employment and performance-forfeiture conditions.
evidence: . Ryder does not argue that the Retention Agreement is ambiguous, but rather that she is entitled to receive payment under the Retention Agreement because she is entitled .to FMLA, protection for the absences alleged and, as such, Shell is precluded from relying on those absences in terminating .her employment and denying her the retention payment. This Court does not agree.
reason: The proposed issue concerns whether “affected” and “may” leave the consequences of a position change unclear. The quoted passage expressly characterizes Ryder’s argument as one about FMLA-protected absences and termination—not contractual ambiguity—and nowhere interprets the scope of “affected” or the effect of “may.”

clause_name: Section 2(c) — Forfeiture for performance or misconduct
issue: Forfeiture turns on the Company "conclud[ing]" that "you failed to meet performance expectations," a standard with no defined content and no stated process, and the closing trigger sweeps in any violation of the Code of Conduct "in any respect." Whether these are unreviewable Company judgments or objective conditions is the obvious battleground.
court_defect: The court addressed whether Shell could invoke the performance-expectations forfeiture based on absences Ryder claimed were FMLA-protected, not whether Shell’s conclusion was contractually unreviewable or governed by an objective standard. The court expressly noted that Ryder did not claim the agreement was ambiguous.
evidence: . Ryder does not argue that the Retention Agreement is ambiguous, but rather that she is entitled to receive payment under the Retention Agreement because she is entitled .to FMLA, protection for the absences alleged and, as such, Shell is precluded from relying on those absences in terminating .her employment and denying her the retention payment. This Court does not agree.
reason: The proposed issue concerns ambiguity in “concludes,” undefined performance expectations, lack of process, and the breadth of the Code-of-Conduct trigger. The passage instead identifies the dispute as whether FMLA protection prevented Shell from relying on particular absences; it does not construe the subjective-versus-objective question or the Code-of-Conduct language.

issue: The grant covers "risks of direct physical loss or damage" resulting from "an occurrence," and both "direct physical loss or damage" (does cosmetic or functional impairment count?) and the scope of a single "occurrence" are open to competing readings. This is the core coverage sentence on which any coverage dispute would turn.
court_defect: The court construed whether “physical loss or damage” covers cosmetic physical alterations, such as hail dents, or instead requires functional damage or diminished usefulness. It concluded that the phrase unambiguously includes cosmetic hail damage.
evidence: Against the backdrop of Advance Cable and other persuasive authority that suggests that “physical loss or damage” includes cosmetic hail damage that physically alters an insured’s property, the Court is not convinced that the cases offered by Defendant define the phrase to mean functional damage. At best, Defendant’s authority provides a competing interpretation for “physical loss or damage,” thereby creating ambiguity as to whether this phrase encompasses cosmetic damage. Such an ambiguity would result in the Court interpreting the phrase in Plaintiffs favor to include cosmetic damage. However, the Court has found above that based on a plain and ordinary reading of the “Insuring Agreement” section, the phrase “physical loss or damage” unambiguously includes the cosmetic hail damage to Plaintiffs Covered Property.
reason: The proposed issue expressly identifies competing cosmetic-versus-functional readings of “direct physical loss or damage,” which is exactly what the court considered. The passage does not address the proposal’s separate concern about the scope of a single “occurrence,” but the exact match on the principal phrase warrants high alignment.

issue: The definition is circular: a "covered loss" requires a "peril insured against," which is itself defined as a cause of loss "for which this policy provides coverage."
court_defect: The court construed whether “covered loss,” particularly the term “a loss,” unambiguously limits real-property coverage to functional damage rather than cosmetic damage. It also considered whether that definition limits the broader Insuring Agreement.
evidence: Defendant argues that because courts have defined “a loss” as an “undesirable outcome” or “financial detriment,” the phrase requires an actual functional loss to the property. Plaintiff cites authority suggesting that even cosmetic hail dents create an “undesirable outcome” or a “financial detriment.” Based on this competing authority, the Court finds that the phrase “covered loss” does not unambiguously limit coverage of real property to functional damage.
reason: The proposed issue alleges circularity between “covered loss” and the definition of “peril insured against.” The passage instead addresses whether “a loss” requires functional damage and gives no sign that the court considered the definition of “peril insured against” or any circularity.

clause_name: Section 22.6 — Notice of Sanctions to Accuser
issue: "[A]ny sanctions that relate to them in accordance with applicable laws" leaves both which sanctions relate to the Accuser and which laws govern disclosure unstated.
court_defect: The court construed whether “outcome” and “sanction” mean the same thing or whether sanction is a subset of outcome, as well as whether the panel makes a recommendation or final decision. It did not construe which sanctions “relate to” the Accuser or which “applicable laws” govern disclosure.
evidence: To the extent the Handbook is ambiguous, it concerns (1) whether “outcome” and “sanction” are the same thing, or “sanction” is a subset of “outcome,” and (2) whether the panel makes a “recommendation” or a “final decision.”
reason: The proposed issue targets uncertainty in “relate to them” and “applicable laws.” Although the court quoted that language and analyzed the same section, its identified ambiguity concerned the distinct relationship between “outcome” and “sanction,” not the scope of sanctions relating to the Accuser or the governing disclosure laws.

issue: Immediate effect "regardless of any appeal" contradicts Section 21.1 ("Sanctions shall not take effect until approved"; suspensions and dismissals not until approved by the SSAO/D) and Section 19.7 (sanctions not effective until approved or modified after appeal).
court_defect: The court construed whether “outcome” and “sanction” have the same meaning and whether the panel makes a recommendation or a final decision, in determining whether the panel could revisit the Special Examiner’s responsibility finding. It did not construe when sanctions become effective relative to approval or appeal.
evidence: To the extent the Handbook is ambiguous, it concerns (1) whether “outcome” and “sanction” are the same thing, or “sanction” is a subset of “outcome,” and (2) whether the panel makes a “recommendation” or a “final decision.” Neither ambiguity, however resolved, addresses the finality of the Special Examiner’s “responsibility” finding.
reason: The proposed issue alleges a timing conflict between immediate effectiveness and other provisions delaying sanctions pending approval or appeal. Although the court quoted the immediate-effect sentence, it used the text to analyze different ambiguities—terminology and decision-making authority—and gave no sign that it considered the alleged timing conflict.

clause_name: Section 22.6 — Appeal of Panel’s Final Decision
issue: The right to appeal "the final decision by the panel" cannot be reconciled with the Panel definition and Deliberations Phase, under which the panel only recommends, and with the statement that "[t]he SSAO/D will render the final decision as to any outcomes".
court_defect: The court construed the inconsistency between language making the panel’s role recommendatory and the appeals language describing the panel as making a “final decision.”
evidence: To the extent the Handbook is ambiguous, it concerns (1) whether “outcome” and “sanction” are the same thing, or “sanction” is a subset of “outcome,” and (2) whether the panel makes a “recommendation” or a “final decision.”
reason: The proposed issue identifies the conflict between the panel’s elsewhere-stated recommendation role, the SSAO/D’s final-decision authority, and the appeal clause’s reference to a panel “final decision.” The court expressly identifies that same recommendation-versus-final-decision ambiguity, differing only in calling it an ambiguity rather than irreconcilable.

issue: Barring appeals grounded in "dissatisfaction with an imposed sanction" is hard to square with the appeal right granted over the panel's outcome decision, which is the sanction itself, and with the UAB's charge to address "the specific concerns of the Appellant".
court_defect: The court found that § 22.6’s appeal language contributes to ambiguity over whether an “outcome” is the same as a “sanction” or broader than a sanction, and whether the panel makes a recommendation or a final decision. It did not identify a conflict involving the UAB’s charge to address the appellant’s specific concerns.
evidence: Furthermore, in describing the “Appeals Procedures,” .section 22.6 states that “[t]he Accuser and the Accused are entitled to appeal the final decision by the panel in the Special Examiner Process to the University Appeals Board ... Appeals shall not be based upon, or granted due to, dissatisfaction with an imposed sanction.” (Id. § 22.6 at 46-47) (emphasis added). According to that language, the panel actually makes a “final decision,” and again the term “sanction,” rather than “outcome,” is used.
reason: The proposed issue and the court both engage with the juxtaposition of the appeal right and the sanction bar, particularly the relationship between an “outcome” and a “sanction.” But the court treats that language as evidence of terminology and decision-maker ambiguities, not expressly as a contradiction that nullifies the appeal right, and it does not discuss the proposed UAB-charge conflict.

issue: The report "makes a finding about whether the Accused is responsible", but the text does not say whether that finding is itself the adjudication or merely a recommendation.
court_defect: The court construed whether the Special Examiner’s responsibility finding was final or instead subject to reexamination or revision by the panel. It also distinguished that question from the separate ambiguity over whether the panel makes a recommendation or a final decision.
evidence: Here, the Handbook clearly delineates between a finding of “responsibility” on the one hand and an “outcome” and/or “sanction” on the other. The finding of “responsibility” is entrusted entirely to a single person — the Special Examiner — and the panel is provided no authority to reexamine or revise that determination. To the extent the Handbook is ambiguous, it concerns (1) whether “outcome” and “sanction” are the same thing, or “sanction” is a subset of “outcome,” and (2) whether the panel makes a “recommendation” or a “final decision.” Neither ambiguity, however resolved, addresses the finality of the Special Examiner’s “responsibility” finding.
reason: The proposed issue asks whether the Special Examiner’s finding is an adjudication or merely a recommendation. The court directly addressed the finding’s finality and held that responsibility was entrusted entirely to the Special Examiner and could not be reexamined by the panel, making this substantially the same defect.

issue: Making the Special Examiner the finder of responsibility cannot be squared with the SSAO/D definition, which makes the SSAO/D responsible for "rendering the final decision", or with the Appeals Procedures' "final decision by the panel".
court_defect: The court construed whether the Handbook’s references to the SSAO and panel making a “final decision” conflicted with the Special Examiner’s authority to determine responsibility. It resolved the apparent inconsistency by distinguishing responsibility findings from outcomes or sanctions.
evidence: Here, the Handbook clearly delineates between a finding of “responsibility” on the one hand and an “outcome” and/or “sanction” on the other. The finding of “responsibility” is entrusted entirely to a single person — the Special Examiner — and the panel is provided no authority to reexamine or revise that determination. To the extent the Handbook is ambiguous, it concerns (1) whether “outcome” and “sanction” are the same thing, or “sanction” is a subset of “outcome,” and (2) whether the panel makes a “recommendation” or a “final decision.” Neither ambiguity, however resolved, addresses the finality of the Special Examiner’s “responsibility” finding.
reason: The proposed issue identifies an apparent conflict between the Special Examiner’s responsibility finding and the “final decision” authority assigned elsewhere to the SSAO or panel. The court expressly construed that same apparent conflict, although it rejected the proposed reading by holding that the final-decision language did not disturb the Special Examiner’s responsibility finding.

issue: The panel is said to "make recommendations as to the outcome(s)", which cannot be squared with the Appeals Procedures' description of an appeal from "the final decision by the panel".
court_defect: The court construed an internal inconsistency over whether the panel merely makes a “recommendation” or instead makes a “final decision,” specifically noting the Appeals Procedures’ reference to the panel’s final decision.
evidence: Furthermore, in describing the “Appeals Procedures,” .section 22.6 states that “[t]he Accuser and the Accused are entitled to appeal the final decision by the panel in the Special Examiner Process to the University Appeals Board ... Appeals shall not be based upon, or granted due to, dissatisfaction with an imposed sanction.” (Id. § 22.6 at 46-47) (emphasis added). According to that language, the panel actually makes a “final decision,” and again the term “sanction,” rather than “outcome,” is used.
reason: The proposed issue identifies the conflict between the panel’s role to “make recommendations” and the Appeals Procedures’ reference to its “final decision.” The passage expressly engages with that same textual conflict and concludes that the language creates ambiguity about whether the panel recommends or finally decides.

issue: "Upon voting, the panel will communicate its recommendations" describes an advisory vote, in tension with the Appeals Procedures, which treat the panel as having made a "final decision".
court_defect: The Handbook is internally ambiguous about whether the panel merely makes a recommendation or instead makes a final decision, because the Appeals Procedures characterize the panel’s action as final.
evidence: To the extent the Handbook is ambiguous, it concerns (1) whether “outcome” and “sanction” are the same thing, or “sanction” is a subset of “outcome,” and (2) whether the panel makes a “recommendation” or a “final decision.”
reason: The proposed issue identifies the conflict between the panel’s advisory “recommendations” and the Appeals Procedures’ “final decision” language. The court expressly identifies that same recommendation-versus-final-decision ambiguity.

issue: "The SSAO/D will render the final decision as to any outcomes" directly contradicts the Appeals Procedures, which give the parties a right to appeal "the final decision by the panel".
court_defect: Section 22.6 inconsistently describes the panel as making recommendations while the SSAO/D renders the final outcomes decision, yet the Appeals Procedures refer to the panel itself as making a “final decision.” The court expressly identified this as an ambiguity over whether the panel makes a recommendation or a final decision.
evidence: Furthermore, in describing the “Appeals Procedures,” .section 22.6 states that “[t]he Accuser and the Accused are entitled to appeal the final decision by the panel in the Special Examiner Process to the University Appeals Board ... Appeals shall not be based upon, or granted due to, dissatisfaction with an imposed sanction.” (Id. § 22.6 at 46-47) (emphasis added). According to that language, the panel actually makes a “final decision,” and again the term “sanction,” rather than “outcome,” is used.
reason: The proposed issue identifies the same conflict the court addressed: the SSAO/D is assigned the final outcomes decision, while the Appeals Procedures call the panel’s decision final. clause_name: Section 9 — Initial Cost of Insurance Rates

evidence: However, the Court does not find that these two phrases create any ambiguity regarding the word “retainer” as used in section 4.1 of the Contract, nor that they become nullities if the Court accepts Xenophon’s interpretation, of section 4.1 of the Contract as a flat fee monthly retainer. clause_name: Section 6.1 — Modification or Stopping of Work
issue: If the Client may stop all work under 6.1 while remaining liable to pay under 4.1's monthly retainer, this provision is hard to reconcile with section 2.2's 60-day termination right, which would become the only way to end payment. Which provision governs a total stoppage is unresolved.

clause_name: Section V(J) — Insured vs. Insured Exclusion

clause_name: Section 18.10 — Texhoma assignment of rights and obligations
issue: The clause lets Texhoma assign "its rights and obligations hereunder to any entity" with notice to PEG, but does not say whether notice is a condition of effectiveness or whether the assignment releases Texhoma from its own obligations. Both the effect of the assignment on the assignor and the meaning of "assign its obligations" are open to opposing readings.

It held that the provision did not terminate Texhoma Fiber’s continuing liability upon assignment.

reason: The proposed issue’s concern about whether assigning obligations releases Texhoma is exactly what the court decided, including the clause’s silence about termination of the assignor’s obligations. The proposed notice-as-condition issue was not decided, but its separate concerns about the effect of assignment and the meaning of assigning obligations align directly with the court’s analysis.

clause_name: Section 18.10 — Texhoma assignment of rights and obligations

The court construed that silence as leaving Texhoma Fiber bound, particularly by the non-circumvention obligation.

issue: "Accelerate" is not defined, and the sentence does not say whether it bars only a demand for the discounted present value of the remaining term or also a judgment for future rent as it falls due.
court_defect: The court construed whether the prohibition on acceleration prevents the landlord from recovering unaccrued future rent as anticipatory-breach damages, including rent characterized as present-value damages. It held that future rent had not ripened and only past-due rent could be recovered.

Glenzan Associates, Inc., 75 A.D.2d 660, 426 N.Y.S.2d 347 (3rd Dept.1980). This is the issue currently before the Court, and Plaintiff has presented no authority which would convince the Court to hold otherwise. While Plaintiff may be entitled to damages other than future rents as a result of Defendant’s alleged breach, Defendant’s motion to dismiss Plaintiffs breach of contract claim for future rents is granted.

The court directly resolved that scope by holding that the right to future rent had not ripened, recovery was limited to past-due rent, and the future-rent claim must be dismissed.

clause_name: Amendment No. 2 to Section 9.5(b) — Default in Payment

issue: The contribution base — "8% of each employee's pay rate per shift for each shift worked by each employee in the bargaining unit" — leaves both "employee in the bargaining unit" and "pay rate per shift" undefined, and caps contributions at five shifts "in any payroll week in any one Office." Paying "8% of each employee's pay rate per shift for each shift worked" could be reasonably read to mean monetary contribution rate of 8% of earnings or, in other words, the total payments over the total shifts.

But the court addressed whether the base unit was shifts or wages, not the proposed questions about casuals, extras, non-members, or work at another office.

issue: The royalty is one-eighth of "the price paid to Lessee" per thousand cubic feet, followed by struck-through language that would have allowed deduction of post-production costs for gathering, transportation, dehydration, extraction and compression; whether striking that language bars such deductions, or merely leaves the point silent, is the central ambiguity. "The price paid to Lessee" also fixes neither the point of sale nor the arm's-length character of the sale.
court_defect: The court construed whether “marketed and used off the premises,” particularly in light of the deletion of the post-production-cost language, imposes an express duty to bring gas to marketable form and sell it off-premises rather than merely identifying royalty-bearing gas. It also considered whether a low-price wellhead transfer to an affiliate satisfies that language.
evidence: To "market" under Plaintiffs' leases may well mean to incur post-production costs to prepare gas for sale, based on the fact that the original parties crossed out the language "less or net any post production costs paid by the Lessee to prepare for and/or deliver the [gas] for sale[,]" but retained the marketing language. This understanding of "marketed" would impose on Equinor a duty to reduce gas to marketable form and sell it at a price higher than it would command "at the wellhead"-or, a duty to market. Supporting that understanding is the fact that the leases appear to equate "marketed and used off the premises" (Leases § 4(B) ) with "marketed and sold off the premises (id. § 6 (emphasis added) ), and gas transferred at the wellhead to an affiliate is not sold "off the premises."
reason: The proposed issue and the passage both focus on the legal effect of striking the post-production-cost language and on the inadequacy of the clause to specify an acceptable sale point or affiliate transaction. The court frames those concerns as an ambiguity in “marketed” and a possible express duty to market, rather than directly deciding whether deductions themselves are barred, so the match is strong but not exact.

issue: Subparagraph (A) promises oil royalty "free of cost" while subparagraph (C) directs the Lessee to deduct the Lessor's share of severance and other taxes from the (A) and (B) payments, so the lease elsewhere both forbids and mandates deductions from royalty. That tension bears directly on whether post-production costs may be netted.
court_defect: The court construed whether § 4(B)’s retained word “marketed,” together with the deletion of its post-production-cost deduction language, creates an express duty to prepare gas for market and obtain a downstream price, notwithstanding the lease’s disclaimer of implied duties. It did not construe a conflict between subparagraphs (A) and (C).
evidence: To "market" under Plaintiffs' leases may well mean to incur post-production costs to prepare gas for sale, based on the fact that the original parties crossed out the language "less or net any post production costs paid by the Lessee to prepare for and/or deliver the [gas] for sale[,]" but retained the marketing language. This understanding of "marketed" would impose on Equinor a duty to reduce gas to marketable form and sell it at a price higher than it would command "at the wellhead"-or, a duty to market.
reason: Both issues concern whether post-production deductions are permissible, but they identify different textual defects. The proposed issue relies on an alleged conflict between (A)’s “free of cost” language and (C)’s tax deductions, whereas the court focused on the deletion of deduction language from (B) and the retained term “marketed”; it never addresses the proposed (A)/(C) conflict.

issue: "Lessee shall be required to maintain a well density of at least 1 well per 160 acres contained in such unit" is susceptible of being read as an affirmative obligation to drill one well for every 160 acres, or merely as a constraint on how a unit may be formed; "maintain" fixes no date by which the density must be achieved, and "such unit" takes its content from the pooling sentence it was lifted from. Each reading yields a different result on breach.
court_defect: The court construed whether “such unit” makes the well-density requirement applicable to all development units or only larger units required by law. It also construed whether “per 160 acres” requires another well for a partial additional 160-acre increment.
evidence: What is clear is that the well density provisions are patently ambiguous as to whether they apply to all development units. Starting with Plaintiffs' proffered interpretation, the fact that 160 divides into 640 neatly is a sign that the well density requirement may apply to units of not more than 640 acres. And "such unit" may refer to both smaller and larger units: the omission of the modifier "larger" could indicate "such unit" is used in a broad sense rather than a narrow one, encompassing all development units.
reason: The proposed issue and the court both identify a contextual scope problem involving “such unit” and the surrounding unitization language. But the court’s specific dispute was whether the requirement covered all units or only larger state-required units, not whether it was a drilling obligation rather than a unit-formation constraint, and the court did not address the proposed timing defect in “maintain.”

issue: Read as a drilling obligation the sentence contradicts paragraph 7, which reserves to the Lessee the right "of drilling or not drilling on the leased premises ... as the Lessee may elect," and paragraph 20, which forbids reading any implied covenant or obligation into the lease. Harmonising all three is precisely what a court would be asked to do.
court_defect: The court construed whether the well-density requirement applies to all development units or only larger units required by law, and whether “at least 1 well per 160 acres” requires two wells on a 300-acre unit. It did not construe an asserted conflict with the lessee’s drilling-election right or the prohibition on implied obligations.
evidence:
All of that is to say, at this early stage, it is unclear if the well density requirement applies to the 300-acre Wootten North Unit at issue. Plaintiffs and Defendants have proffered reasonable but conflicting interpretations of the unitization clauses. Thus, Plaintiffs' claims for breach of the unitization and habendum clauses survive, but only if it is clear or at least ambiguous that the well density requirement would require the Wootten North Unit to have at least two wells.
2. The well density requirement
The next dispute is accordingly over the meaning of the well density requirement. Again, the parties are at odds. Plaintiffs insist that "at least 1 well per 160 acres" means a 300-acre unit cannot have just one well, because that creates a ratio of one well to 300 acres. (Doc. 42 at 15-16). Defendants respond that "per 160 acres" means "for each 160-acre group ," which in turn means a 300-acre unit has one 160-acre group to which the density requirement applies and one 140-acre group to which it does not. (See Doc. 39 at 12-14).
reason: The proposed issue concerns a conflict between Section 8 and paragraphs 7 and 20 over whether Section 8 creates a drilling obligation. The passage instead addresses which units are covered and how the one-well-per-160-acres formula operates, without engaging the alleged conflicts with paragraphs 7 or 20.

issue: The sentence says the Termination Value "will reflect changes in the market value of the parties' respective positions (including any embedded derivatives) and may be volatile", without tying "market value" to the Agreement's defined Market Value. The measure it announces is left undefined.

Barclays has not shown how the Market Value of the MBS enters into that calculation.

issue: "Termination Value" turns on what a hypothetical "Dealer of recognized standing" "would be willing to pay" and on what is "necessary to compensate the non-defaulting party fairly", all as determined "in good faith". Each standard is open-textured and controls the size of the number.
court_defect: The provision gives the non-defaulting party, acting as Calculation Agent, unilateral authority to calculate Termination Value subject to good faith, leaving a factual question whether unexplained inputs and unusually large discrepancies satisfy that standard. The court also considered whether the Repo Unwind Charge had any contractual basis under the Termination Value provision.
evidence: The thrust of Barclays’ argument in support of summary judgment is that, as Calculation Agent, Barclays was contractually vested with the unilateral right to calculate Termination Value. See Confirmation at 5 (“For purposes of determining the Termination Value in connection with the occurrence of an Event of Default, the Calculation Agent will be the nondefault-ing party.”); id. at 3 (“ ‘Termination Value’ shall mean the amount, determined by the Calculation Agent in good faith.... ”). Thus, the only question before the Court is whether Barclays acted in good faith in making its calculation.
reason: The court directly engaged with the proposed issue’s concern that the open-ended “good faith” standard governs the Calculation Agent’s unilateral determination and therefore the amount charged. But it did not treat “necessary to compensate ... fairly” or “Dealer of recognized standing” as independently vague or construe their possible meanings, so the alignment is substantial but incomplete.

issue: The clause appoints Barclays itself to determine the Termination Value used in its own margin calls without stating any standard in the clause. What constrains that self-interested determination must be found elsewhere.
court_defect: The court construed whether naming Barclays as Calculation Agent for Termination Value also authorized it to determine unilaterally the underlying Market Value used in the margin-call process. It held that the designation did not necessarily confer that authority because the MRA assigned Market Value determination to an agreed, generally recognized source.
evidence: Moreover, even if the Market Value of the MBS was an input into the calculation of Termination Value or otherwise impacted Termination Value, as Barclays claims is suggested by page 1 of the Confirmations, cited earlier, that would not necessarily make Barclays the sole determiner of Market Value. Just because Barclays has the right to put the numbers into the calculator to determine the strength of its position does not mean that, as a matter of law, Barclays has the unilateral right to determine those numbers. Instead, the MRA expressly gave that right to a “generally recognized source agreed to by the parties.”
reason: The proposed issue and the passage both concern whether Barclays’ Calculation Agent designation permits an unconstrained, self-interested determination and whether other contract text supplies the constraint. The match is not exact because the court specifically distinguished calculating Termination Value from unilaterally determining Market Value, rather than addressing an absence of standards governing Barclays’ calculation of Termination Value itself.

issue: "Market Value" turns on a "price ... obtained from a generally recognized source agreed to by the parties or the most recent closing bid quotation from such a source", leaving open both what qualifies as a generally recognized source and what happens when no source has been agreed; the trailing "unless contrary to market practice" adds a further undefined override. For illiquid mortgage securities two parties can plausibly reach very different values on this wording.
court_defect: The MRA requires Market Value to come from a “generally recognized source agreed to by the parties,” but neither the MRA nor the Confirmations identifies that source. The court construed whether Barclays could nevertheless act unilaterally as the source and concluded that the source’s identity depended on disputed extrinsic evidence.
evidence: In sum, the MRA provides that Market Value must be determined by a “generally recognized source agreed to by the parties,” but the MRA and Confirmations do not specify that source. The parties certainly could have named such a source in the contract, but nothing in the plain language of the MRA or the Confirmations makes Barclays the “generally recognized source.”
reason: The proposed issue expressly identifies the failure to specify an agreed generally recognized source and the uncertainty if none was agreed, which is the central defect the court addressed. The court did not separately construe the proposed issue’s broader uncertainty about what sources qualify or its characterization of the trailing market-practice language, but the specified-source omission is an exact match.

clause_name: Paragraph 11(d)(i) — Default liquidation and retained-security credit
issue: The liquidation remedy is governed by "in a recognized market (or otherwise in a commercially reasonable manner) at such price or prices as the nondefaulting party may reasonably deem satisfactory", and alternatively by a price "obtained from a generally recognized source" chosen in the party's "sole discretion"; each of those standards is contestable and they pull in different directions. A defaulting seller and a liquidating buyer can read the same words to permit and to forbid the same sale or mark.
court_defect: The court construed whether a sale in a “recognized market” automatically satisfies Paragraph 11(d)(i), or whether the sale must still be commercially reasonable and conducted in good faith. It also construed whether BWIC-generated prices qualified as prices from a “generally recognized source” for securities Barclays retained.
evidence: However, Thornburg argues, id.: “Regardless of whether the collateral is sold in a recognized market ... the defaulting party is required to conduct a commercially reasonable liquidation.” Paragraph 11(d) of the MRA provides that, in the event of a default, the nondefaulting party may “immediately sell” the MBS “in a recognized market (or otherwise in a commercially reasonable manner).... ” This language seems to suggest that a sale in a recognized market is per se commercially reasonable. However, in light of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, the better interpretation of the MRA is that a sale in a recognized market is presumptively commercially reasonable, subject to rebuttal of that presumption.
reason: The proposed issue identifies tension among the recognized-market and commercial-reasonableness standards, and the court expressly construed whether the former makes a sale per se reasonable or merely presumptively reasonable. Alignment is not complete because the proposal also broadly challenges “reasonably deem satisfactory” and “sole discretion,” which the court did not separately construe as ambiguous.

issue: The identical venue provision appears in Section 7(2) of the License Agreement, so a dispute spanning both instruments must be allocated between two separately worded but overlapping clauses. Their coexistence is more duplicative than contradictory.
court_defect: The passage construes the substantive scope of the forum-selection clauses—particularly whether the claims seek to “enforce” the 2008 or 2010 agreements or “relate” to the 2012 agreement. It does not treat duplication between the clauses as creating an allocation problem.
evidence: In order for one of ARPwave's claims to fall within the scope of one of the forum-selection clauses, either (1) that claim must be brought "for the enforcement of [the 2008 or 2010] Agreement" or (2) that claim must be a claim "relating to [the 2012] agreement or any related agreements."
reason: Both the proposed issue and the passage concern multiple forum-selection clauses across the agreements, and the court considers their scopes together. But the proposed defect is duplication and allocation between overlapping clauses, whereas the court addresses whether particular claims fall within differently phrased scope language, not whether the clauses conflict or redundantly coexist.

issue: The clause duplicates Section 21 of the Equipment Lease in slightly different words, so a single dispute arising under both halves of the instrument is governed by two overlapping venue provisions. The duplication is awkward rather than contradictory.
court_defect: The court construes whether ARPwave’s claims fall within the differing scopes of several forum-selection clauses—particularly whether they seek enforcement of the 2008 or 2010 agreements. It does not address whether this provision awkwardly duplicates an Equipment Lease provision or creates overlapping venue requirements.
evidence: In order for one of ARPwave's claims to fall within the scope of one of the forum-selection clauses, either (1) that claim must be brought "for the enforcement of [the 2008 or 2010] Agreement" or (2) that claim must be a claim "relating to [the 2012] agreement or any related agreements."
reason: The passage recognizes multiple forum-selection clauses and compares their wording and scope, which is related to the proposed issue’s concern about parallel clauses. But the court addresses which claims each clause covers, not the alleged duplication and overlapping venue governance between this clause and Section 21 of the Equipment Lease.

issue: The clause speaks of "this Agreement" although it appears in the Lease, which paragraph 18 defines as a separate instrument from the License Agreement that carries its own identical venue clause. Which document's disputes are covered has to be worked out across the two.
court_defect: The court construes whether patent-infringement claims fall within the clause’s requirement that an action be brought “for the enforcement of” the 2008 or 2010 agreement. It does not address whether “this Agreement” ambiguously refers to the Lease or the separate License Agreement.
evidence: As ARPwave conceded at oral argument, its patent-infringement claims are not brought to "enforce" the 2008 or 2010 agreements. Those agreements do not even mention the patents, much less require defendants not to infringe them.
reason: The proposed issue concerns which of two related instruments is denoted by “this Agreement,” while the quoted discussion concerns whether patent-infringement claims seek to enforce either agreement. Although both involve the clause’s scope, the passage gives no sign that the court engaged with the asserted Lease-versus-License conflict.

issue: "All actions or proceedings relating to this Agreement or any related agreements" leaves both the reach of "relating to" (tort, trade-secret and non-party claims) and the undefined phrase "any related agreements" open, and the clause mixes consent to jurisdiction with a mandatory "must be litigated" venue command.
court_defect: The court construed the scope of “relating to,” deciding whether patent-infringement claims had a sufficient connection, relevance, or reference to the 2012 agreement or related agreements. It concluded they did not because adjudicating those claims would not require reference to or interpretation of the agreements.
evidence: For a patent-infringement claim to "relate" to the 2012 agreement (or to any other agreement), that claim must concern the agreement or have some sort of relevance, connection, or reference to the agreement.
reason: The proposed issue and the court address the same phrase and underlying uncertainty about how far “relating to” extends, although the proposal lists tort, trade-secret, and non-party claims while the court considers patent claims. The court only lightly addresses which agreements are “related” and does not engage with the alleged jurisdiction-versus-venue drafting conflict, so alignment is substantial but partial.

issue: The forum clause binds "each party", but the instrument never names the Licensee other than as "you" in the opening grant, so whether it binds the individual signatory or his company must be resolved from elsewhere in the document.
court_defect: The court construed the scope of “relating to this agreement or any related agreements,” specifically whether patent-infringement claims had a sufficient connection to the agreements to trigger the forum-selection clause.
evidence: For a patent-infringement claim to "relate" to the 2012 agreement (or to any other agreement), that claim must concern the agreement or have some sort of relevance, connection, or reference to the agreement.
reason: The proposed issue concerns uncertainty over which person or entity is bound as “each party.” The passage instead construes the clause’s subject-matter scope through the words “relate” and “related agreements,” with no indication that the court considered the identity of the Licensee or whether the individual or company was bound.

issue: "[T]otal proceeds from a sale, less reasonable expenses, holding costs and expenses relating to transactions regarding the property (i.e. donations, etc)" is vague at every deduction: "reasonable expenses," "holding costs," and an open-ended "etc" catch-all illustrated by a mis-used "i.e." The parenthetical's examples cannot fix the reach of "expenses relating to transactions regarding the property."
court_defect: The court construed whether the term "etc." gives the definition of profit a broad reach across different types of property transactions, while finding that a separate sale-of-real-property trigger limits plaintiffs’ entitlement. It did not construe the meaning of "reasonable expenses" or "holding costs."
evidence: The inclusion of the term "etc." in defining the types of transactions that may generate profit suggests that the parties intended a wide interpretation of the type of transactions that could generate profit.
reason: The proposed issue and the court both engage with the open-ended reach created by "etc." in the transaction-related language. Alignment is partial because the proposal frames this principally as ambiguity in deductible expenses and also challenges "reasonable expenses," "holding costs," and the use of "i.e.," none of which the court construed.

issue: The clause pays "Consultant" — singular — twenty percent, though the Agreement defines two "Consultants," so it is unclear whether 20% is the aggregate or due to each. "[S]ale of a portion or all" also leaves unstated how Profit is allocated to a partial sale.
court_defect: The court construed whether the phrase “sale of a portion ... of Delta Bluffs” encompasses a sale of timber, focusing on whether timber is part of the real property or instead constitutes goods under the UCC. It also construed the relationship between that triggering language and the Agreement’s broad definition of profit.
evidence: The Agreement entitles plaintiffs to a portion of the "sale of a portion ... of Delta Bluffs." ECF No. 19-1 at 1. And because, under the UCC, the sale of timber is a sale of goods, it is not a sale of a portion of Delta Bluff's real property.
reason: The proposed issue concerns whether 20% is aggregate or payable to each Consultant and how profit is allocated following a partial sale. The court did address the same “sale of a portion” phrase, but it construed whether a timber transaction qualifies as such a sale, not allocation mechanics or the singular “Consultant,” so the defects are related but materially different.

issue: The sentence is a comma splice joining a permissive statement ("Company or its principal may realize certain tax savings") to a payment obligation, and the trigger — "once the risk of a federal or state tax audit has expired, which is expected to occur in October 2016" — states an expectation rather than a date. It is also unclear whether savings realized by "its principal," a non-party, obligate the Company.
court_defect: The court construed the provision’s payment trigger—whether the risk of a tax audit had actually expired—and treated October 2016 as an anticipated expiration rather than the operative deadline. It did not address the comma splice or whether savings realized by the Company’s principal obligated the Company.
evidence: The Agreement states that plaintiffs are entitled to 20% of Delta's tax savings "once the risk of a federal or state tax audit has expired." ECF No. 19-1 at 1. The Agreement anticipates the risk to expire in October 2016. Id.
reason: The proposed issue and the court both distinguish the actual expiration-of-audit-risk trigger from the expected October 2016 timing, so that component is clearly aligned. The proposed issue’s separate concerns about sentence mechanics and the non-party principal do not appear in the court’s analysis.

issue: The capital obligation is measured only by "an amount that DMSA deems appropriate" and the parenthetical lets DMSA count its own travel, legal, accounting and internal "labor of management and staff" as contributed capital. Both the existence of any minimum obligation and what may be booked as capital (and later repaid ahead of members under paragraph 4) are open to competing readings.
court_defect: The court construed whether “an amount that DMSA deems appropriate” gave DMSA unlimited discretion over the nature and extent of its capital contribution, potentially making the obligation indefinite or illusory. It ultimately held that the discretion did not eliminate the obligation and that compliance required fact-finding.
evidence:
Notwithstanding this factual dispute, Plaintiffs contend that summary judgment is appropriate since DMSA could hardly have breached an agreement that only required it to contribute an amount that it deemed “appropriate.” While the plain language of the Venture Agreement appears to favor Plaintiffs’ position, the courts of Maine have long held that one party’s “ ‘reservation ... of an unlimited right to determine the nature and extent of [its] performance’ renders the obligation too indefinite to be enforceable.” Larson v. Johnson, 184 F.Supp.2d 26, 32 (D.Me.2002) (citing Corthell v. Summit Thread Co., 132 Me. 94, 167 A. 79, 81 (1933)).
Of course, the fact that the Venture Agreement appears to provide DMSA with unbridled discretion to determine the nature of its contribution does not make the contract unenforceable per se.
reason: The proposed issue’s concern that the clause specifies no minimum beyond what DMSA itself deems appropriate directly matches the court’s analysis of DMSA’s apparently unlimited discretion and the possible indefiniteness of its obligation. The passage also addresses the nature and amount of DMSA’s contribution, but it does not specifically construe the parenthetical’s list scope or the paragraph 4 repayment consequence.

issue: Clause (c) permits "the use or transfer of money or Cash Equivalents in a manner that is not prohibited by the terms of this Agreement" — a circular catch-all sitting alongside six tightly specified dispositions, so its reach is set only by whatever else the Agreement happens not to forbid. Clause (e) compounds this by permitting sales of Notes Receivable "for a cash purchase price of not less than eighty (80%) of the unpaid balance," a figure whose unit is left out.
court_defect: The court construes clause (e)’s malformed “eighty (80%)” language as requiring a cash purchase price of at least eighty percent of the unpaid balance, supplying “[percent]” and applying that threshold to a face-value sale.
evidence: LSA § 7.13 exempted transfers designated as “Permitted Dispositions,” which' LSA § 1.1 defined as “a sale of a Note Receivable ... for a cash purchase price of not less than eighty [percent] (80%) of the unpaid balance.... ” Dkt. 17-1, Ex. 6 at 15, 51. R.E. Loans sold the secured notes to MF08 at face value in exchange for cash, so the sales constituted “Permitted Dispositions” and were thus exempt from LSA § 7.13.
reason: The proposed issue specifically identifies the missing unit after “eighty,” and the court’s bracketed insertion of “[percent]” shows it construing that same wording defect as an eighty-percent threshold. The passage does not address the separate circular-catch-all criticism concerning clause (c), but exact alignment with the clause (e) defect is sufficient for a high score.

issue: Clause (ii) requires deposit of "all of their Collections" into an account "in Fund's name," while clause (iii) separately requires sale and payoff proceeds of Notes Receivable to be remitted by the escrow or title company to a Cash Management Account — leaving it uncertain whether such proceeds are "Collections" and what happens to Manager's own receipts in an account held only in Fund's name. The obligations are cast on the Borrowers but the operative money movement depends on third parties.
court_defect: The court considered whether Wells Fargo’s control over revenues and expenditures through § 2.6’s lockbox supported an inference that it actually knew MF08’s financial condition. It did not construe whether note-sale proceeds qualify as “Collections,” whose receipts must be deposited, or how third-party payment obligations operate.
evidence: Uecker fails to explain how maintaining control over R.E. Loans ’ revenues and expenditures pursuant to LSA § 2.6’s “lockbox” provision gave Wells Fargo actual knowledge of MF08’s financial condition.
reason: The proposed issue concerns the scope of “Collections,” accounts in Fund’s name, and dependence on third parties. The passage invokes § 2.6 only to assess whether lockbox control implied knowledge of MF08’s condition, without engaging any of those asserted ambiguities.

issue: The subsection purports to impose the primary obligation on non-parties — "Each Cash Management Bank shall establish and maintain Cash Management Agreements with Lender and each Borrower" — without saying that the Borrowers must procure it, so whose breach a failure is remains open. The required term (iii), a daily sweep of "all amounts in the applicable Cash Management Account," is likewise stated as the bank's undertaking rather than the Borrowers'.
court_defect: The passage does not show the court construing any drafting defect in Section 2.6(b). It considers only whether Wells Fargo’s control under Section 2.6’s lockbox arrangement supported an inference that Wells Fargo knew of MF08’s financial condition.
evidence: Uecker fails to explain how maintaining control over R.E. Loans ’ revenues and expenditures pursuant to LSA § 2.6’s “lockbox” provision gave Wells Fargo actual knowledge of MF08’s financial condition.
reason: The proposed issue concerns whether Section 2.6(b) improperly places obligations on nonparty Cash Management Banks and leaves responsibility for failure unclear. The court instead addressed whether the lockbox control evidenced Wells Fargo’s knowledge, without discussing who owed the contractual duties or whose breach nonperformance would constitute.

issue: After two specific prohibitions — transfers of property to an Affiliate (a) and acquisitions of Notes Receivable from an Affiliate (b) — clause (c) sweeps in "any other transaction between such Borrower and any Affiliate," subject only to four soft conditions ("ordinary course," "fair and reasonable terms," "fully disclosed," "no less favorable ... than ... arm's length"). The reach of that general catch-all against the enumerated specifics, and the expanded 10% "Affiliate" test that applies only for this Section, are both open to argument.
court_defect: The court construed whether § 7.13 applied to the sales between R.E. Loans and MF08, concluding that it did not because the sales qualified as exempt “Permitted Dispositions.”
evidence: In addition, the bankruptcy court properly found that LSA § 7.13’s restrictions did not apply to the transfers from MF08 to R.E. Loans. See Dkt. No. 17-1, Ex. 2 at 16-17. LSA § 7.13 exempted transfers designated as “Permitted Dispositions,” which' LSA § 1.1 defined as “a sale of a Note Receivable ... for a cash purchase price of not less than eighty [percent] (80%) of the unpaid balance.... ” Dkt. 17-1, Ex. 6 at 15, 51.
reason: The proposed issue concerns the scope of clause (c)’s “any other transaction” catch-all relative to clauses (a) and (b), plus a section-specific Affiliate threshold. The court instead construed the separate opening exemption for “Permitted Dispositions” and gave no sign that it addressed either proposed ambiguity.

issue: "Sponsored Investment Fund" sweeps in any fund "sponsored, promoted, owned or managed now or in the future by the Manager or its Affiliates" and names R.E. Loans, LLC expressly, so the label attaches to the Manager's own affiliated vehicles. Whether that status was meant to strip such entities of affiliate treatment is genuinely contestable.
court_defect: The court construed whether § 5.1(c)’s express inclusion of R.E. Loans as a “Sponsored Investment Fund” excluded loans to R.E. Loans from treatment as related-party loans under § 5.7(e). It held that the exclusion applied and that the related-party lending restrictions therefore did not govern those loans.
evidence: However, pursuant to the final paragraph of NPA § 5.7(e), a related party loan did not include “any loan in which the borrower or co-borrower is a Sponsored Investment Fund....” Dkt. No. 17-1, Ex. 4 at 15. NPA § 5.1(c), in turn, expressly defined “Sponsored Investment Fund” to include R.E. Loans. Id. at 9. Therefore, the loans made by MF08 to R.E. Loans were not subject to the restrictions in NPA § 5.7(e) because R.E. Loans was a “Sponsored Investment Fund.”
reason: The proposed issue questions whether designation as a Sponsored Investment Fund strips an affiliated vehicle such as R.E. Loans of affiliate-related treatment. The court addressed that exact interaction, holding that R.E. Loans’ expressly defined status excluded loans to it from the related-party-loan restrictions, although it rejected the proposed issue’s suggestion that the language was contestable.

clause_name: Section 5.7(e)(ii) — Related Party Loan Portfolio Cap
issue: The cap is set at twenty percent "of the Loan Portfolio", a term defined in 5.4(a) as the aggregate principal of outstanding Portfolio Loans measured monthly, so the denominator and the moment of measurement are not obviously the same as "immediately after making or purchasing". How the cap is computed is genuinely open.
court_defect: The court construed whether § 5.7(e)(ii)’s cap applied to loans made to R.E. Loans. It held that those loans were excluded because R.E. Loans was expressly defined as a “Sponsored Investment Fund.”
evidence: However, pursuant to the final paragraph of NPA § 5.7(e), a related party loan did not include “any loan in which the borrower or co-borrower is a Sponsored Investment Fund....” Dkt. No. 17-1, Ex. 4 at 15. NPA § 5.1(c), in turn, expressly defined “Sponsored Investment Fund” to include R.E. Loans. Id. at 9. Therefore, the loans made by MF08 to R.E. Loans were not subject to the restrictions in NPA § 5.7(e) because R.E. Loans was a “Sponsored Investment Fund.” Accordingly, NPA § 5.7(e)(ii)’s proscription of related party loans in excess .of twenty percent of MF08’s loan portfolio did not apply to the loans from MF08 to R.E. Loans.
reason: The proposed issue concerns a potential mismatch between the cap’s immediate measurement time and the monthly measurement used to define its denominator. The court instead construed whether the particular loans were categorically excluded from § 5.7(e); it did not address how or when the twenty-percent denominator should be calculated.

issue: The exclusion removes from "Related Party Loan" any loan whose borrower is a Sponsored Investment Fund or Private Client, categories defined in 5.1(b)-(c) to include entities owned or managed by the Manager. Whether such a loan is nonetheless a loan to an "Affiliate" under 5.7(e) is precisely the kind of question a court is asked to resolve.
court_defect: The court construed whether the specific exclusion for loans whose borrower is a Sponsored Investment Fund removes those loans from § 5.7(e)’s restrictions on loans to affiliates. It held that the exclusion applied because R.E. Loans was expressly defined as a Sponsored Investment Fund.
evidence: NPA § 5.7(e) prohibited MF08 from making a loan to an “affiliate” (designated as a “related party loan”) unless the loan met certain conditions: NPA § 5.7(e)(i) required that related party loans satisfy the same underwriting standards customarily applied by MF08 in other transactions and NPA § 5.7(e)(ii) prohibited related party loans made in excess of twenty percent of MF08’s total loan portfolio. TAC ¶ 41; Dkt. No. 17-1, Ex. 4 at 14-15. However, pursuant to the final paragraph of NPA § 5.7(e), a related party loan did not include “any loan in which the borrower or co-borrower is a Sponsored Investment Fund....” Dkt. No. 17-1, Ex. 4 at 15. NPA § 5.1(c), in turn, expressly defined “Sponsored Investment Fund” to include R.E. Loans. Id. at 9. Therefore, the loans made by MF08 to R.E. Loans were not subject to the restrictions in NPA § 5.7(e) because R.E. Loans was a “Sponsored Investment Fund.”
reason: The proposed issue identifies the interaction between the general treatment of affiliate loans as Related Party Loans and the specific Sponsored Investment Fund/Private Client exclusion. The court directly construed that interaction for the Sponsored Investment Fund branch, although it did not address Private Clients or separately decide whether R.E. Loans remained an Affiliate.
