clause_name: Section 1 — Amendment of PETROLEUM ARGUS application
issue: The first paragraph of the amended identification runs "...relating to stocks and bonds in electronic format downloadable from and made available via a global computer network on a subscription basis" with no punctuation, so it is unclear whether the trailing "in electronic format downloadable..." qualifies the excluded asset-management material or the publications being claimed. The first item also carries no International Class designation while the other two are expressly placed "in Class 16" and "in Class 36".
court_defect: The court construed whether the provision’s exclusion for “asset management and investment advice relating to stocks and bonds” prohibited Argus Media from publishing stock prices, and more broadly whether an obligation concerning registration also restricted use of the marks. It held that publishing stock prices was not the excluded advice and that the agreement did not constrain use.
evidence: Instead, the disclaimer Argus Media added to its registration application refers to providing “information concerning asset management and investment advice relating to stocks and bonds.” Publishing stock prices is simply not the same as providing “asset management and investment advice relating to stocks.”
reason: The proposed issue concerns the syntactic scope of “in electronic format downloadable...” and the first item’s missing class designation. The court instead construed the substantive meaning of the asset-management/investment-advice exclusion; it did not address either the modifier-scope ambiguity or the omitted class designation.

issue: After the specific undertakings "not oppose or seek to cancel" the application, the clause adds the open-ended catch-alls "otherwise contest or challenge" the rights and "do any act or thing in derogation thereof", leaving it genuinely uncertain whether Argus Research also surrendered infringement or unfair-competition claims outside the PTO. It is further unclear whether the limitation "for the goods and services as set forth in that application as amended" qualifies only the mark "as shown" or the entire non-challenge promise.
court_defect: The court construed whether the Agreement’s registration-focused promises also restricted use of the named marks, including use beyond the scope of their registrations. It held that the Agreement addressed registration only and did not constrain either party’s use.
evidence: The Court also rejects Argus Research’s claim that the Agreement sought to limit the use of the “PETROLEUM ARGUS” and “ENERGY ARGUS & Design” marks to the scope of the registrations. As the Court noted above, the unambiguous language of the contract speaks only to registration, and does not constrain use of the marks by either party.
reason: The proposed issue and the court both address whether Section 2’s registration-related language reaches conduct involving use outside the PTO and outside the registration’s scope. The alignment is not exact because the proposed issue focuses on the catch-alls, their grammatical scope, and surrender of infringement or unfair-competition claims, while the court does not expressly parse those words or discuss those causes of action.

clause_name: Section 3 — Non-opposition to ENERGY ARGUS & Design
issue: The clause protects "Petroleum Argus' rights in the mark ENERGY ARGUS" while the registrations it identifies are for "ENERGY ARGUS & Design", so it is ambiguous whether Argus Research gave up challenges to the composite marks only or to the words ENERGY ARGUS standing alone. The trailing catch-all "do any act or thing in derogation thereof" sits against the enumerated "oppose or seek to cancel" and leaves the covenant's outer reach uncertain.
court_defect: The court construed whether the non-opposition covenant extended beyond the specifically named registered marks to other ARGUS marks or regulated use of the named marks. It concluded that the agreement covered only the named marks and did not constrain use.
evidence: In return, Argus Research agreed not to oppose, seek to cancel, or otherwise interfere with Argus Media’s “PETROLEUM ARGUS” and “ENERGY ARGUS & Design” marks. There simply is no language in the Agreement to suggest that the parties intended to say anything about future registrations of other “ARGUS” marks, or intended to limit use in any particular way, and the Court thus rejects Argus Research’s breach of contract claims regarding any marks other than “PETROLEUM ARGUS” or “ENERGY ARGUS & Design.”
reason: The proposed composite-mark-versus-word-mark concern substantially overlaps the court’s determination that the covenant covered “ENERGY ARGUS & Design” but not other ARGUS marks. However, the court did not expressly analyze the clause’s reference to “the mark ENERGY ARGUS” or the list-scope effect of “do any act or thing in derogation thereof,” so the alignment is partial.

clause_name: Section 4.10(a) — Submission to Jurisdiction and Venue
issue: The consent is that proceedings 'may be instituted in or (other than by the Guarantor) removed to' the New York courts, permissive language coupled with an asymmetric parenthetical; whether the New York forum is exclusive as against the Guarantor is not stated. The clause is one-sided enough that any genuine ambiguity would be read against the drafting lenders.
court_defect: The court construed whether the clause’s use of “may,” despite the guarantor’s venue and forum-non-conveniens waivers, made the designated New York forums permissive rather than mandatory. It held that the clause became mandatory once the plaintiff filed in a designated forum.
evidence: Based upon their plain meaning, the Court concludes that the clauses at issue here are mandatory or, more precisely, became mandatory once Plaintiff had filed suit in one of the designated fora. It is true that the first portion of the clauses, which states that “any legal action, suit or proceeding .. .may be instituted in or (other than by the Guarantor) removed to the U.S. federal and New York state courts located in the Borough of Manhattan, City and State of New York,” e.g., Phua Decl., Ex. 7, at 11 (§ 4.10) (emphasis added), is phrased in a permissive fashion. That portion must not be read in isolation, however, because the remaining portion of the clauses changes the nature of the parties’ bargain:
reason: The proposed issue and the court both focus on whether “may be instituted in or (other than by the Guarantor) removed to” creates only permissive forum selection or instead binds the guarantor to the selected New York forum. Alignment is not complete because the court resolved that question through the separate waiver language and did not address the proposed contra-drafter point or independently analyze the parenthetical’s asymmetry.

clause_name: Section I.C.1 — Right of First Refusal
issue: The Right of First Refusal is defined by reference to "any or all of the period from the expiration of the automatic renewal term ... through two years thereafter", leaving unclear whether it reaches offers negotiated during the term for post-term capacity. "Bona fide offer" and "exclusive right to match" are also undefined.
court_defect: The court construed whether the ROFR’s temporal scope turns on when an offer is made or when the proposed lease would commence.
evidence: Nextel’s claim that Section I.C.3 was breached presupposes that (1) the ROFR applies to any lease of the DC Spectrum whenever the offer to lease was made between February 21, 2005 and February 21, 2007, regardless of when the lease would commence; and (2) Clearwire made such an offer to HITN between February 21, 2005 and February 21, 2007. The ROFR, however, grants Nextel a right of first refusal only with respect to an offer to lease the DC Spectrum to commence between February 21, 2005 and February 21, 2007.
reason: The proposed issue specifically questions whether offers made during the relevant period for post-term capacity trigger the ROFR, and the court directly resolved that offer-date-versus-commencement-date issue. The passage does not address the additional complaints that “bona fide offer” and “exclusive right to match” are undefined, but the central temporal defect is an exact match.

clause_name: Section I.C.2 — Notice of Proposed Lease
issue: The notice is required "at the commencement of any negotiations", with no stated consequence for failing to give it. The trigger "desires to enter into an agreement" is a state of mind rather than an observable event.
court_defect: The court construed whether the ROFR’s applicability depended on when an offer was made or when the proposed lease would commence. It held that the relevant event was commencement of the lease within the specified two-year period.
evidence: Nextel’s claim that Section I.C.3 was breached presupposes that (1) the ROFR applies to any lease of the DC Spectrum whenever the offer to lease was made between February 21, 2005 and February 21, 2007, regardless of when the lease would commence; and (2) Clearwire made such an offer to HITN between February 21, 2005 and February 21, 2007. The ROFR, however, grants Nextel a right of first refusal only with respect to an offer to lease the DC Spectrum to commence between February 21, 2005 and February 21, 2007.
reason: The proposed issue concerns the subjective phrase “desires to enter into an agreement” and the absence of a stated consequence for failing to provide notice. The court instead addressed offer timing versus lease-commencement timing, giving no sign that it construed either proposed defect.

issue: "[T]erms or conditions that have the purpose or the effect of preventing ENET from exercising its Right of First Refusal" is open-ended; almost any term a third party demands could be said to have that effect. The provision gives no standard for measuring effect.
court_defect: The court construed whether Section I.C.3 prohibited agreements concerning a lease that would commence after the underlying ROFR’s two-year effective period. It held that no agreement could “prevent” exercise of the ROFR when the ROFR did not apply to the contemplated lease.
evidence: The Royalty Agreement simply did not grant such an extensive right; the ROFR ceased to bind HITN after February 21, 2007. Thus, because Clearwire never made an offer to lease excess DC Spectrum capacity from HITN by a lease to commence on a date between February 21, 2005 and February 21, 2007, it was impossible for HITN to accept any offer that could have prevented Nextel from exercising its ROFR to lease excess DC Spectrum capacity during the 2-year ROFR period.
reason: The proposed issue concerns the alleged vagueness and potentially limitless causal reach of “purpose or the effect of preventing.” The court applied that language but resolved the dispute through the ROFR’s temporal scope, not by addressing the lack of a standard for measuring a term’s preventive effect.

clause_name: Section 2 — Managing Agent duties and indemnity
issue: The section contains mechanical errors that change meaning: two different subparagraphs are both lettered "(d)" (the $1,000 spending cap and the separate-account duty), so later cross-references to lettered subparagraphs are indeterminate, and the indemnity in (i) covers acts "admitted to be taken" where "omitted" is plainly meant. A court asked to apply the indemnity or a cross-reference would have to correct the text.
court_defect: The court construed a potential conflict between the indemnification clause and the separate insurance-obligation clause, holding that the more specific insurance obligation takes priority. It did not construe typographical errors within Section 2.
evidence: The Management Agreement’s insurance obligation clause is more specific than the indemnification clause, and the Court finds that in the event the two clauses would be inconsistent, the insurance obligation clause is primary.
reason: The proposed issue concerns duplicate subparagraph lettering and the apparent substitution of “admitted” for “omitted.” The passage instead addresses the indemnity clause’s priority relative to a separate insurance clause and gives no sign that the court considered either mechanical error.

clause_name: Section 2 — Managing Agent duties and indemnity
issue: Subparagraph 2(i)'s indemnity of the Principal against Managing Agent negligence is hard to square with Paragraph 3(c), which obliges the Principal to carry liability insurance naming the Managing Agent as additional insured against claims arising from management and operation of the Buildings. Which party bears a negligence loss is left genuinely uncertain.
court_defect: The court construed the potential inconsistency between the Managing Agent’s indemnification obligation and the Principal’s obligation to obtain insurance covering the Managing Agent. It resolved that conflict by holding the more specific insurance obligation primary.
evidence: Indiana law is clear that an insurance obligation clause shifts the risk of loss from either party, including Hokanson, to an insurance company. The Management Agreement’s insurance obligation clause is more specific than the indemnification clause, and the Court finds that in the event the two clauses would be inconsistent, the insurance obligation clause is primary.
reason: The proposed issue identifies uncertainty created by the conflict between Section 2(i)’s indemnity and Paragraph 3(c)’s insurance obligation. The passage directly construes that same conflict and determines which clause controls, so the fact that the court resolves the uncertainty rather than leaving it open does not diminish the near-exact alignment.

issue: The amount of cover is left to "such reasonable amount as the Principal shall determine", combining a self-judging discretion with an objective reasonableness standard. If the Managing Agent were left uninsured for a claim, the adequacy of the Principal's determination is precisely what a court would construe.
court_defect: The court construed the potential conflict between the insurance-obligation clause and the indemnification clause, determining which clause controlled. It did not construe the Principal’s discretion to determine a “reasonable amount” of insurance.
evidence: The Management Agreement’s insurance obligation clause is more specific than the indemnification clause, and the Court finds that in the event the two clauses would be inconsistent, the insurance obligation clause is primary.
reason: The proposed issue concerns ambiguity in the amount-of-coverage standard and the Principal’s discretion, whereas the passage addresses the insurance clause’s priority over a potentially inconsistent indemnification clause. Although both involve the same provision, they concern different alleged defects.

issue: The Principal's duty to insure the Managing Agent as additional insured pulls against the Managing Agent's indemnity of the Principal in Paragraph 2(i), but the two can be harmonised as covering negligence and non-negligence losses respectively. No squarely contradictory provision was found.
court_defect: The court construed the potential inconsistency between the Principal’s obligation to insure the Managing Agent and the Managing Agent’s obligation to indemnify the Principal. It resolved that conflict by treating the insurance obligation as more specific and therefore primary.
evidence: Indiana law is clear that an insurance obligation clause shifts the risk of loss from either party, including Hokanson, to an insurance company. The Management Agreement’s insurance obligation clause is more specific than the indemnification clause, and the Court finds that in the event the two clauses would be inconsistent, the insurance obligation clause is primary.
reason: The proposed issue and the court address the same two clauses and the same potential conflict between insurance and indemnification obligations. The alignment is not perfect because the proposal harmonizes them based on negligence versus non-negligence losses, whereas the court applies specificity and primacy if they are inconsistent.

issue: The term clause says the Agreement "shall continue until December 31, 2010, and shall continue in effect until either party terminates" on ninety days' notice, which can be read either as a fixed two-year term or as an evergreen agreement terminable at will. The two readings produce opposite results on whether termination after 2010 requires any reason at all.
court_defect: The court construed the scope of the opening phrase “Subject to Section 12”: whether it conditions all Section 2 termination rights or only the term through December 31, 2010. That determination controlled whether either party could terminate without cause on ninety days’ notice after that date.
evidence: On the other hand, the Defendant’s interpretation gives effect to all of the language in Section 2 of the 2009 Agreement by making termination subject to the conditions set forth in “Section 12” until December 31, 2010, while preserving the parties’ right to terminate the agreement upon 90 days’ written notice for any reason after December 31, 2010.
reason: The proposed issue matches the court’s engagement with whether Section 2 permits no-cause termination after December 31, 2010. But it frames the textual defect as fixed-term versus evergreen language, whereas the court specifically treated it as a scope dispute over whether “Subject to Section 12” modifies the post-2010 termination right.

issue: Section 2 lets either party terminate on ninety days' notice with no reason stated, while Section 12(i) permits ninety-day termination only "for good cause" or on a change in COMPANY's business; the two cannot both be the exclusive route out. Section 2's opening "Subject to Section 12" does not resolve which prevails.
court_defect: The court construed whether Section 2’s opening phrase, “Subject to Section 12,” applies to all termination rights in Section 2 or only to termination through December 31, 2010. This determined whether Section 2 permitted termination without cause on ninety days’ notice after that date despite Section 12’s limited grounds.
evidence: Here, the parties agree that “Subject to Section 12” imposes a condition precedent. However, they disagree as to how broadly the parties intended for it to apply to the termination rights set forth in Section 2. The Plaintiff contends that the parties intended the language, “Subject to Section 12,” to make all of the termination rights set forth in Section 2 subject to the conditions set forth in Section 12. (The Pl.’s Mem. of Law at 10.) The Defendant argues that the parties only intended, “Subject to Section 12,” to apply to the first clause of the first sentence in Section 2, “this Agreement shall become effective as of the date hereof shall continue until December 31, 2010,” and not the second clause, “and shall continue in effect until either party terminates this agreement by providing the other party with written notice of termination at least ninety (90) days prior to. such termination.” (The Def.’s Mem. of Law at 10.)
reason: The proposed issue identifies the precise dispute the court construed: whether Section 2’s general ninety-day termination right is constrained by Section 12 and whether “Subject to Section 12” resolves that relationship. The court expressly compared those competing readings and ultimately harmonized them by treating Section 12 as controlling through December 31, 2010 and Section 2 as allowing without-cause termination afterward.

issue: Requiring good cause and ninety days' notice cannot be reconciled with Section 2, which lets either party terminate on ninety days' notice without any cause, nor with 12(ii) and 12(iii), which permit immediate termination or termination after a five-business-day cure period. The three termination regimes give inconsistent answers to the same facts.
court_defect: The court construed whether Section 12’s cause-based termination rights could be harmonized with Section 2’s post-2010 right to terminate without cause on 90 days’ notice, including Section 12(iii)’s separate five-day termination mechanism.
evidence: Construing -Section 2 to, afford either party the right to terminate the 2009 Agreement without cause after December 31, 2010 does not affect or otherwise inhibit a party’s right to terminate the 2009 Agreement based on the conditions set forth in Section 12 at any point after the Agreement becomes effective. See Morse/Diesel, Inc. v. Trinity Indus., Inc., 67 F.3d 435, 439 (2d Cir.1995) (“[T]he entire contract must be considered, and all parts of it reconciled, if possible, in order to avoid an inconsistency.”) (quoting Cruden v. Bank of New York, 957 F.2d 961, 976 (2d Cir.1992)). For example, Section 12(iii) gives the Defendant the right to terminate the Agreement if the Plaintiff fails to cure a material breach after five days written notice. (Ceruto Deck, Ex. A, at 11.) If the Court were to adopt the Defendant’s interpretation of Section 2, the Defendant would have (i) the right to terminate the 2009 Agreement within five days under Section 12 if the Plaintiff fails to cure a material breach; and (ii) have the right terminate the 2009 Agreement pursuant to Section 2 of the Agreement on 90 days’ notice without cause after December 31, 2010. There is nothing inconsistent about affording the Defendant the right to terminate the 2009 Agreement under these distinct and separate circumstances.
reason: The proposed issue identifies conflicts among Section 12(i), Section 2’s no-cause 90-day right, and Section 12’s accelerated termination provisions. The court squarely construed that coherence question and specifically compared Section 2 with Section 12(iii), although it found the regimes consistent and did not separately analyze Section 12(ii).

issue: "Excess of underlying insurance which afford limits not less than the limits specified" leaves open whether a self-insured retention counts as "underlying insurance" and what happens if the underlying limits fall short. The phrase is a condition of attachment with no stated consequence for non-compliance.
court_defect: The court construed whether Article I limits the Reinsurance Agreement to OHIC’s excess liability policies or also reaches its primary policies. It did not construe whether a self-insured retention is “underlying insurance” or the consequences of underlying limits falling short.
evidence: Under the “APPLICATION OF AGREEMENT” provision of the Reinsurance Agreement (Article I), the agreement applies to hospital professional liability coverage under certain excess liability policies of OHIC. The Umbrella Policy fits squarely within this provision, while the Primary Policy does not. Nothing in the “application of agreement” provision suggests that the agreement applies, in any way, to any of OHIC’s primary policies.
reason: The passage construes Article I’s excess-versus-primary policy scope. The proposed issue instead concerns the distinct phrase requiring underlying insurance with minimum limits, specifically self-insured retentions and noncompliance consequences, neither of which the court addresses.

issue: "Loss" is confined to amounts "actually paid by the REINSURED" and "within applicable policy limits," yet sub-paragraph (b) covers amounts paid in excess of policy limits, so the opening restriction and the enumerated items pull against each other. Whether payment must precede the reinsurer's obligation is left open.
court_defect: The court construed whether the phrase “within applicable policy limits” excluded prejudgment interest for which OHIC was directly liable, notwithstanding Article IV’s express inclusion of prejudgment interest. It held that the interest remained a covered loss because OHIC’s liability arose from its policies and was calculated on the covered portion of the verdict.
evidence: Despite the reference to prejudgment interest in the definition of loss, ERC seems to argue that the prejudgment interest imposed here under § 807.01(4) is not covered because OHIC was directly liable for payment of the interest. In this regard, ERC asserts that the “within applicable policy limits” language of the definition of “loss” indicates an intent to only cover payments under applicable insurance policies. ERC views the definition of loss as only covering OHIC’s payments made on behalf of its insured pursuant to its policy obligations and not sums for which it is directly liable.
reason: The proposed issue and the court both implicate “within applicable policy limits” and amounts paid by OHIC, but they identify different defects. The court addressed policy-based versus direct liability for prejudgment interest; it did not address any conflict between subparagraph (a)’s within-limits language and subparagraph (b)’s excess-of-limits coverage, or whether prior payment was a condition precedent.

clause_name: Article IV — Definition of Claim Expenses
issue: "[A]llocated investigation, adjustment, and legal expenses" and "the supplementary payments provisions of the REINSURED'S policy" are undefined, so the line between allocated (reimbursable) and unallocated expense is left to argument. The "including" list is illustrative, not exhaustive.
court_defect: The court construed whether “the REINSURED’S policy” referred to both the Primary Policy and Umbrella Policy or only to the reinsured excess policy. It concluded that claim expenses were covered only when incurred by OHIC in its capacity as an excess insurer.
evidence: OHIC argues that the phrase “all payments under the supplementary payments provisions of the REINSURED’S policy” in the definition of claim expenses refers to the supplementary payments provisions of the Primary Policy and the Umbrella Policy, not just the Umbrella Policy.
reason: The court construed the policy-level referent and scope of the same “supplementary payments provisions” phrase. The proposed issue instead focuses on the distinction between allocated and unallocated expenses and whether the “including” list is exhaustive, neither of which the passage shows the court addressing.

clause_name: Article V — Indemnity for Claim Expenses
issue: The proviso indemnifies claim expenses "connected with such settlement or appeal," but no settlement is mentioned anywhere in the proviso — the antecedent is missing, so what expenses fall inside the special ratio is uncertain. The main pro-rata formula also does not say whether claim expenses sit within or in addition to the Article III limits.
court_defect: The court construed whether Article V covers claim expenses paid under OHIC’s primary policy or only expenses incurred in OHIC’s capacity as an excess insurer. It concluded that Article V’s reference to “reinsurance afforded by the other terms of this agreement” limits coverage to the latter.
evidence: By referring to “reinsurance afforded by the other terms of this agreement,” the provision addressing indemnification for claim expenses in effect references the reinsurance provided under Article III, which concerns “loss sustained by the REINSURED” under the excess policies described in Article I. Therefore, the Reinsurance Agreement unambiguously demonstrates an intent that OHIC would only be indemnified for “claim expenses” incurred in its capacity as an excess insurer.
reason: The proposed issue concerns the missing antecedent for “such settlement” and whether claim expenses are within or additional to Article III’s limits. The court instead used Article V’s opening qualification and its relationship to Articles I and III to decide whether primary-policy expenses were covered; it did not construe either proposed defect.

clause_name: Article IX — Joint Participation in Claims
issue: "[I]n the judgment of the CORPORATION" commits the trigger for joint participation to one party's opinion, and "participate jointly" does not say who controls the defence or settlement. Its fit with the REINSURED's duty to settle or defend under c033 is left to inference.
court_defect: The court construed whether “REINSURED” in Article IX included OHIC acting in any capacity or only in its capacity as an excess insurer. It did not construe ERC’s unilateral judgment trigger or determine who controlled defense or settlement.
evidence: OHIC argues that, under the limited construction of the term “REINSURED” advocated by ERC, ERC only has the right to participate jointly in the defense of a claim if the reinsured is defending the claim in its capacity as an excess insurer. Even so, OHIC, in its capacity as the excess insurer, and ERC, as the reinsurer of the Umbrella Policy, obviously had interest in the Hegarty litigation insofar as damages potentially exceeded the Primary Policy limits. The court does not read this provision to suggest a construction of the term “REINSURED” to include OHIC, acting in any capacity, throughout the Reinsurance Agreement.
reason: The proposed issue concerns the phrase “in the judgment of the CORPORATION,” control over defense or settlement, and interaction with another duty. The passage instead addresses the capacity-based scope of “REINSURED”; its reference to joint defense does not engage with discretion or control.

issue: "Ultimate net loss" excludes all loss and legal expenses yet is defined as "the sum actually paid or payable in cash," leaving the treatment of amounts payable but unpaid open. Whether settlements without the company's written consent count is likewise unresolved on the face of it.
court_defect: The court construed whether the exclusion for “interest on any judgment” encompasses prejudgment interest or only interest accruing after judgment. It resolved the phrase’s temporal ambiguity by holding that it refers only to postjudgment interest.
evidence: But the use of the words “on any judgment” reasonably indicates an intent to only exclude, from the definition of ultimate net loss, interest that accumulates after the judgment is entered. While postjudgment interest begins to accumulate only after judgment is entered, prejudgment interest is calculable when judgment is entered and therefore typically forms part of the judgment.
reason: The proposed issue concerns amounts that are payable but unpaid and settlements entered without written consent. The court instead construed the distinct phrase “interest on any judgment” and did not address either paid-versus-unpaid amounts or lack of consent.

issue: The clause directs division into "two (2) equal parts, one of which shall be distributed to each of Grantor's children, Mark Andrew Scott and Paul Ethan Scott, and any later children born of Grantor's marriage", which cannot work if there is a later-born child: a fixed two-way split contradicts an open class of takers. It is also unclear whether the later-born class, and the trigger "upon Grantor's death if Grantor's wife shall predecease him", fix the shares as of the Grantor's death or the wife's.
court_defect: The court construed whether “Grantor’s wife” in the death-trigger clause referred specifically to Sarah Oneida Covington Scott or instead to a current or future wife. It held that the phrase referred to Sarah throughout the sentence.
evidence: The clause, “upon Grantor’s death if Grantor’s wife shall predecease him” is immediately preceded, within the same sentence, by the clause, “[u]pon the death of Grantor’s wife, Sarah Oneida Covington Scott.” A common sense, fair, and “plain meaning” interpretation of this sentence indicates that “Grantor’s wife,” as used through the entire sentence, refers to “Sarah Oneida Covington Scott.”
reason: The proposed issue concerns the conflict between a fixed two-part division and an open class of children, plus uncertainty about when shares are fixed. Although the court construed the same death-trigger language, it addressed the identity of “Grantor’s wife,” not the number of shares, the open class, or the time at which beneficiaries’ shares are fixed.

clause_name: Part III — Enhanced Yield Fund Cash Redemption
issue: The postponement/suspension right must be reconciled with the preceding sentence giving Shareholders the right to require redemption "no less often than as of the close of each Business Day" and with the Fund's daily-liquidity objective in Investment Objectives. The document never states which prevails.
court_defect: The court construed a conflict between the Confidential Memoranda’s requirement that redemption be in cash and Declaration § 5.2’s grant of discretion to redeem shares in cash or securities. It did not address whether postponement or suspension conflicted with daily redemption rights or the Fund’s liquidity objective.
evidence: Similarly, with respect to redemption of Trust shares, Section 5.2 of the Declaration gave the Trustee discretion to redeem Trust shares in cash or securities, whereas the Confidential Memoranda for the two Funds provide that redemption would be in cash. Again, resolving the conflict between these terms is an issue of fact and so summary judgment is not appropriate.
reason: Both concern coherence between the redemption provision and other contract terms, but they identify different conflicts. The proposed issue concerns the timing or suspension of redemption versus daily liquidity, while the court addressed the form of redemption—cash versus securities.

clause_name: Part III — Enhanced Yield Fund Liability Limitation
issue: The cover legend states that "no legal liability is assumed or is to be implied against" Wells Fargo or its agents with respect to the Memorandum, an unqualified disclaimer, whereas this clause expressly preserves liability for negligence. The two liability statements are not aligned.
court_defect: The court construed this provision as imposing a simple-negligence liability standard that conflicted with the Declaration’s gross-negligence standard when the transaction documents were read together.
evidence:
Similarly, in other documents, Wells Fargo assumed responsibility for negligent conduct. See Confidential Memorandum for the EY Series, Exh. A-4 to Def.’s Mot. for Summ J., ECF No. 294-4 (“Wells Fargo ... shall have no liability to the Trust or the Shareholders for any act or omission, provided that such act or omission does not involve bad faith, willful misconduct, negligence or reckless disregard of its duties to the Trustee”) (emphasis added).
Considering the documents together, I conclude there is an ambiguity in the conflict between the “gross negligence” standard of the Declaration and the simple negligence standard of the SLA and other documents.
reason: Both issues concern this provision’s negligence standard conflicting with another liability statement. But the proposed issue identifies the cover legend’s unqualified disclaimer, whereas the court addressed the different conflict between this provision’s simple-negligence standard and the Declaration’s gross-negligence standard; the passage does not mention or construe the cover legend.

clause_name: Part V — Enhanced Yield Fund Investment Objective
issue: The safety-of-principal and daily-liquidity objective is in tension with the operative guidelines permitting five-year maximum maturities, 15% illiquid securities and asset-backed and mortgage-backed holdings. Whether the objective constrains the guidelines or merely aspires is unresolved.
court_defect: The court construed whether investments expressly authorized by the investment guidelines could nonetheless breach the agreement by failing to satisfy the separate “prime considerations” of principal safety and liquidity. It concluded that those considerations constrained investments otherwise permitted by the guidelines.
evidence: Wells Fargo first argues that the collateral investments were all authorized by the investment guidelines because the Trustee was authorized to purchase “mortgage backed securities,” “asset-backed securities,” and “debt obligations.” It argues that the securities issued by Lehman, Cheyne, and Stanfield were debt obligations and therefore authorized. However, if these investments, while meeting the letter of the guidelines, did not comply with the “prime considerations” of “safety of principal and liquidity requirements” they would nonetheless be out of compliance with the SLA and could amount to a breach of that agreement.
reason: This directly addresses the proposed conflict between the safety-and-liquidity objective and operative authorization of mortgage-backed, asset-backed, and debt securities, and it resolves the objective-versus-aspiration question by treating the prime considerations as constraints. The passage does not specifically discuss the proposed issue’s five-year maturity or 15% illiquidity examples, so the alignment is slightly short of complete.

clause_name: Part V(b) — Enhanced Yield Fund Permitted Investments
issue: The list is headed "Portfolio Diversification" yet imposes no diversification requirement, and it authorises long-dated categories that sit against the "(a) Portfolio Quality" highest-short-term-rating limit and the safety/daily-liquidity objective. The permitted categories and the quality gate are not harmonised.
court_defect: The court construed the permitted-investment categories as not independently dispositive: investments authorized by category could still violate the SLA if they conflicted with the overarching safety-of-principal and liquidity requirements.
evidence: Wells Fargo first argues that the collateral investments were all authorized by the investment guidelines because the Trustee was authorized to purchase “mortgage backed securities,” “asset-backed securities,” and “debt obligations.” It argues that the securities issued by Lehman, Cheyne, and Stanfield were debt obligations and therefore authorized. However, if these investments, while meeting the letter of the guidelines, did not comply with the “prime considerations” of “safety of principal and liquidity requirements” they would nonetheless be out of compliance with the SLA and could amount to a breach of that agreement.
reason: This directly matches the proposed conflict between the listed permitted categories and the safety/liquidity objective. The passage does not address the separate complaints about the “Portfolio Diversification” heading or the highest-short-term-rating limit, so the alignment is strong but not complete.

clause_name: Part III — CI Term Trust Cash Redemption
issue: The reserved right to postpone payment or suspend redemptions sits against the stated purpose of the Trust (c003) to give securities lenders a continuous, daily-liquid source of managed investment and against the daily-liquidity investment objective (c039). A court could be asked whether the suspension power can be exercised so as to defeat those stated terms.
court_defect: The court construed a conflict between the Confidential Memoranda’s requirement that redemption be in cash and the Declaration’s grant of discretion to redeem in cash or securities. It also separately noted that the segregated-account wind-down might violate contractual liquidity requirements.
evidence: Similarly, with respect to redemption of Trust shares, Section 5.2 of the Declaration gave the Trustee discretion to redeem Trust shares in cash or securities, whereas the Confidential Memoranda for the two Funds provide that redemption would be in cash. Again, resolving the conflict between these terms is an issue of fact and so summary judgment is not appropriate. Finally, disaggregating the collateral investments into pro rata accounts in which some portions were too small to be sold may violate the contractual requirements of liquidity in the investments.
reason: The proposed issue concerns whether the power to postpone payment or suspend redemptions conflicts with promises of continuous daily liquidity. The court addressed the same redemption provision and liquidity generally, but the specific conflict it construed was cash redemption versus redemption in cash or securities—not suspension or delayed payment defeating daily liquidity.

clause_name: Part III — CI Term Trust Liability Limitation
issue: The exculpation runs to "Wells Fargo and other agents of the Trust" without reference to Wells Fargo's separate roles as Trustee and self-appointed Investment Manager (c008), and it must be read against the Declaration of Trust standards it does not restate. A court could be asked which capacity and which standard governs.
court_defect: The court treats the provision’s simple-negligence carveout as conflicting with the Declaration’s gross-negligence standard, creating ambiguity over which document and liability standard governs. It also considers whether the SLA specifically governs collateral-investment obligations while the Declaration governs the Trustee’s general duties.
evidence:
Similarly, in other documents, Wells Fargo assumed responsibility for negligent conduct. See Confidential Memorandum for the EY Series, Exh. A-4 to Def.’s Mot. for Summ J., ECF No. 294-4 (“Wells Fargo ... shall have no liability to the Trust or the Shareholders for any act or omission, provided that such act or omission does not involve bad faith, willful misconduct, negligence or reckless disregard of its duties to the Trustee”) (emphasis added).
Considering the documents together, I conclude there is an ambiguity in the conflict between the “gross negligence” standard of the Declaration and the simple negligence standard of the SLA and other documents. Resolution of the interplay among these various provisions, and whether any should be given primacy, should be done by a fact-finder.
reason: The proposed issue aligns with the court’s concern that this provision must be read against the Declaration and that the competing liability standards require a determination of primacy. The court does not, however, address the specific alleged failure to distinguish Wells Fargo’s capacities as Trustee and Investment Manager, so the match is substantial but incomplete.

clause_name: Part V — CI Term Trust Investment Objective
issue: The stated premium on safety of principal and daily liquidity is difficult to reconcile with the policies permitting up to 15% in illiquid securities (c046), five-year maturities (c055) and mortgage- and asset-backed paper (c044). A court could be asked whether the objective constrains the permitted-investment list or is overridden by it.
court_defect: The court construed whether investments expressly authorized by the investment guidelines could nonetheless breach the agreement by failing to satisfy the stated “prime considerations” of safety of principal and liquidity.
evidence: Wells Fargo first argues that the collateral investments were all authorized by the investment guidelines because the Trustee was authorized to purchase “mortgage backed securities,” “asset-backed securities,” and “debt obligations.” It argues that the securities issued by Lehman, Cheyne, and Stanfield were debt obligations and therefore authorized. However, if these investments, while meeting the letter of the guidelines, did not comply with the “prime considerations” of “safety of principal and liquidity requirements” they would nonetheless be out of compliance with the SLA and could amount to a breach of that agreement.
reason: This is the same operative conflict the proposed issue identifies: whether the safety-and-liquidity objective constrains investments otherwise permitted by the guidelines. Although the passage does not mention the 15% illiquidity allowance or five-year maturities, it expressly addresses the proposed issue’s mortgage- and asset-backed examples and resolves the broader objective-versus-permitted-list question.

clause_name: Part V(b) — CI Term Trust Permitted Investments
issue: The breadth of the permitted list is hard to reconcile with the Portfolio Quality restriction (c043) that the Trust "may only invest" in obligations with the highest short-term rating, and with the safety-of-principal and daily-liquidity objective in c039. A court could be asked whether the list expands or is cut down by those provisions.
court_defect: The court construed whether investments expressly authorized by the permitted-investments list could nevertheless violate the agreement because they failed to satisfy the separate “prime considerations” of safety of principal and liquidity.
evidence: Wells Fargo first argues that the collateral investments were all authorized by the investment guidelines because the Trustee was authorized to purchase “mortgage backed securities,” “asset-backed securities,” and “debt obligations.” It argues that the securities issued by Lehman, Cheyne, and Stanfield were debt obligations and therefore authorized. However, if these investments, while meeting the letter of the guidelines, did not comply with the “prime considerations” of “safety of principal and liquidity requirements” they would nonetheless be out of compliance with the SLA and could amount to a breach of that agreement.
reason: This directly matches the proposed conflict between the broad permitted-investments list and the safety-of-principal and liquidity requirements: the court held that satisfying the list’s literal terms might not be enough. The passage does not separately address the proposed highest-short-term-rating restriction, so the match is strong but not complete.

issue: The disclaimer that the Trustee is not "bound by current or future laws or customs applicable to trust investments" cannot be squared with Section 3.3, which imposes the ERISA prudent-person standard, or with Section 8.5's preservation of ERISA Part 4 duties. A court would have to decide which governs the Trustee's investment conduct.
court_defect: The court construed whether the Declaration’s general requirement that trust property follow Trustee-established investment objectives conflicted with, or was displaced by, the SLA’s more specific collateral-investment standard requiring safety and liquidity.
evidence: Specifically, the Declaration provides only that Trust property be invested “consistent with the investment objectives established by the Trustee,” whereas the SLA contains the actual standard (“The prime considerations for the investment portfolio shall be safety of principal and liquidity requirements.”). Moreover, the SLA was signed after the Declaration. Therefore, a reasonable jury could conclude that the SLA, not the Declaration, is applicable to the dispute here.
reason: Both concern conflicting investment standards involving Section 3.1, but the proposed issue targets the disclaimer of governing laws and its alleged conflict with Sections 3.3 and 8.5’s ERISA duties. The court instead addressed the investment-objectives language and its relationship to the separate, later SLA’s safety-and-liquidity standard.

issue: Section 5.2's opening grants each Shareholder the right to redeem "at a redemption price per Share equal to their Net Asset Value next determined", which assumes a cash price, while this sentence permits payment wholly or partly in securities. Section 5.3's NAV machinery does not say how in-kind assets are to be valued for this purpose.
court_defect: The court construed a conflict between Section 5.2, which permitted redemption in cash or securities, and the Confidential Memoranda, which stated that redemption would be in cash.
evidence: Similarly, with respect to redemption of Trust shares, Section 5.2 of the Declaration gave the Trustee discretion to redeem Trust shares in cash or securities, whereas the Confidential Memoranda for the two Funds provide that redemption would be in cash. Again, resolving the conflict between these terms is an issue of fact and so summary judgment is not appropriate.
reason: Both concern Section 5.2’s cash-or-securities redemption language, but the proposed issue alleges tension with Section 5.2’s opening and a valuation silence in Section 5.3. The court instead addressed a conflict with the Confidential Memoranda’s cash-redemption requirement, so the defects are related but specifically different.

issue: Liability is preserved only for "bad faith, gross negligence, wilful misconduct or reckless disregard of the duties involved", terms the Declaration nowhere defines, and the carve-out is partly corrupted in the text. Where ordinary negligence ends and "gross negligence" begins is the classic contestable line.
court_defect: The court found Section 8.1 ambiguous because its gross-negligence standard conflicted with related agreements imposing liability for simple negligence. It also construed whether the listed carve-outs were exclusive or merely non-exclusive examples of conduct giving rise to liability.
evidence: Considering the documents together, I conclude there is an ambiguity in the conflict between the “gross negligence” standard of the Declaration and the simple negligence standard of the SLA and other documents. Resolution of the interplay among these various provisions, and whether any should be given primacy, should be done by a fact-finder. In addition, I note that the Declaration’s limitation of liability applies first to “any act performed or omitted by such Covered Person in good faith on behalf of the Trust ... and in a manner reasonably believed to be within the scope of authority conferred on such Covered Person by this Declaration.” There is at a minimum a factual question as to whether that description would include the alleged negligent investment of the collateral in risky securities when such conduct is expressly in conflict with the investment objective set forth in the SLA; there is nothing in the Declaration to indicate that covered persons had the authority to violate their own investment standards. Moreover, the second provision of the limitation (providing that a covered person “shall be liable for any loss, damage or claim incurred by reason of such Covered Person’s bad faith, gross negligence, willful misconduct or reckless disregard of the duties involved in the conduct of his or her office”) could be read as a non-exclusive, rather than exclusive, description, of the type of conduct that will give rise to liability. In that case, there would be no conflict with the negligence standards set forth in the other documents.
reason: Both the proposed issue and the court address whether Section 8.1 limits liability to gross negligence and more culpable conduct rather than ordinary negligence. Alignment is partial because the court located the ambiguity in conflicts with related agreements and possible non-exclusivity, not in undefined terminology or textual corruption, and it did not construe the semantic boundary between negligence and gross negligence itself.

issue: The exculpation cannot be squared with Section 3.3, which makes the Trustee an ERISA fiduciary held to the prudent-person standard, or with Section 8.5, which says Article Eight shall not relieve the Trustee of ERISA Part 4 duties. A court would have to fix which standard governs a Shareholder's claim.
court_defect: The court construed whether Section 8.1’s gross-negligence liability threshold conflicted with the simple-negligence standards in the SLA and other transaction documents, and which provisions should control. It found that interplay ambiguous and left its resolution to the fact-finder.
evidence: Considering the documents together, I conclude there is an ambiguity in the conflict between the “gross negligence” standard of the Declaration and the simple negligence standard of the SLA and other documents. Resolution of the interplay among these various provisions, and whether any should be given primacy, should be done by a fact-finder.
reason: Both concern Section 8.1’s liability threshold conflicting with another standard and the need to determine which standard governs. But the proposed issue identifies Sections 3.3 and 8.5 and their ERISA duties, while the court addressed different texts—the SLA and other transaction documents—and did not discuss those sections or an ERISA conflict.

issue: The sentence purports to "replace" all duties and liabilities "otherwise existing at law or in equity" without identifying which provisions do the restricting or which duties are displaced. The scope of the substitution is left entirely to inference.
court_defect: Section 8.4 does not unambiguously displace all noncontractual duties; displacement applies only when the covered person relied in good faith on a specific Declaration provision that conflicts with a common-law duty. The asserted application failed to identify either the specific provision or the conflicting duty.
evidence: I first examine the effect of Section 8.4. I agree with Plaintiff that this provision does not unambiguously eliminate all non-contractual duties. Rather, it replaces common law duties with contractual duties where two circumstances apply: (1) the covered person has relied in good faith on a specific provision of the Declaration in taking some action and (2) that provision conflicts with a common law duty. As noted by Plaintiff, Wells Fargo does not identify any specific provision it purports to have acted in compliance with in good faith or how that provision conflicts with a common law duty.
reason: The proposed issue identifies uncertainty over which Declaration provisions restrict which otherwise-existing duties. The court directly addressed that same uncertainty by requiring identification of a specific provision and the common-law duty with which it conflicts, although it framed part of the problem as Wells Fargo’s failure to make that showing.

issue: The Bank's unilateral "policy and standard guidelines" power sits awkwardly against Section 8, which places all collateral investment loss on the Participant while allowing the Bank to set the investment parameters. Harmonising the two leaves it unclear whether breach of the list is a Bank risk or a Participant risk.
court_defect: The court construed whether the Participant’s assumption of “collateral investment loss” covered losses caused by the Bank investing in securities that violated the SLA’s investment criteria. Thus, it addressed whether noncompliant investments remained the Participant’s risk or could create Bank liability.
evidence: It further argues that Plaintiff undertook the risk of “collateral deficiency or collateral investment loss” pursuant to the SLA, and therefore any claims based on collateral investment losses are contractually released. I conclude that in this context “operation” is ambiguous and there is an issue of fact whether “collateral investment loss” includes the risk of Wells Fargo investing collateral in securities that did not meet the criteria set forth in the SLA.
reason: The proposed issue identifies uncertainty over whether losses from investments breaching the permitted-investment requirements fall on the Bank or the Participant, which is precisely the ambiguity the court identified. The score is slightly below exact alignment because the court did not specifically address the Bank’s unilateral power to establish or change its “policy and standard guidelines.”

issue: This safety-of-principal duty is hard to square with Section 8, under which the Participant "assumes all risk of loss arising out of ... collateral investment loss". One provision imposes an investment standard on the Bank while the other allocates the resulting loss entirely to the Participant.
court_defect: The court construed whether the Participant’s assumption of “collateral investment loss” also covered losses caused by Wells Fargo investing collateral in violation of the SLA’s safety-of-principal and liquidity criteria. It found that scope presented an issue of fact.
evidence: It further argues that Plaintiff undertook the risk of “collateral deficiency or collateral investment loss” pursuant to the SLA, and therefore any claims based on collateral investment losses are contractually released. I conclude that in this context “operation” is ambiguous and there is an issue of fact whether “collateral investment loss” includes the risk of Wells Fargo investing collateral in securities that did not meet the criteria set forth in the SLA.
reason: The proposed issue identifies the tension between the Bank’s safety-of-principal duty and the Participant’s assumption of collateral investment losses. The quoted passage directly addresses whether that loss-allocation language covers losses resulting from investments that failed to satisfy the SLA’s investment criteria, which is essentially the exact conflict proposed.

issue: The unconditional duty to return collateral to the Borrower sits against the closing sentence of Section 4 giving the Bank "a reasonable time ... to liquidate cash collateral investments", and against Section 8's allocation of collateral investment loss. Timing and shortfall consequences are not reconciled.
court_defect: The court found an ambiguity between Plaintiff’s assumption of collateral-deficiency risk and Wells Fargo’s duty to return collateral, specifically whether a shortfall had to be covered before or after the loaned securities were returned.
evidence: While the SLA provides that Plaintiff assumes the risk of collateral deficiencies, it also provides that Wells Fargo will be responsible for returning the collateral to the borrowers, which could arguably create an ambiguity about whether the shortfall had to be made up before or after the loaned securities were returned.
reason: The proposed issue identifies the same unresolved timing and shortfall conflict between the return obligation and the allocation of collateral-investment loss. The court does not mention the separate reasonable-time-to-liquidate language, but it directly construes the proposed issue’s central conflict over whether shortfall payment precedes or follows return.

issue: "Participant assumes all risk of loss arising out of ... collateral investment loss" states an unqualified assumption of risk with no carve-out on its face, yet "all risk of loss" must somehow accommodate the Bank's own conduct. Whether it covers losses caused by the Bank's investment decisions is precisely the open term.
court_defect: The court construed whether the Participant’s assumption of the risk of “collateral investment loss” extends to losses caused by Wells Fargo’s own investment of collateral in securities that violated the SLA’s criteria. It found that scope ambiguous and requiring factual resolution.
evidence: It further argues that Plaintiff undertook the risk of “collateral deficiency or collateral investment loss” pursuant to the SLA, and therefore any claims based on collateral investment losses are contractually released. I conclude that in this context “operation” is ambiguous and there is an issue of fact whether “collateral investment loss” includes the risk of Wells Fargo investing collateral in securities that did not meet the criteria set forth in the SLA.
reason: The proposed issue asks whether the unqualified assumption of collateral-investment-loss risk covers losses caused by the Bank’s own investment decisions. The court addressed that exact scope question, more specifically focusing on investments that failed to satisfy the SLA’s criteria.

issue: It cannot be squared with the closing sentence of the same Section 8, under which "The Bank assumes the risk of loss arising from negligent and fraudulent operation of its Securities Lending Program", nor with Section 2(f)'s safety-of-principal mandate. One sentence gives the Participant all investment loss, the other gives the Bank losses from its own negligent operation.
court_defect: The court construed the ambiguity between the Participant’s assumption of “collateral investment loss” and Wells Fargo’s liability for negligent “operation” of the program, particularly when collateral was invested contrary to the SLA’s investment criteria.
evidence: Wells Fargo contends that the negligence standard of the SLA does not apply because it imposes liability on Wells Fargo only with respect to the “operation” of the Securities Lending Program, which does not include the investment of the collateral. It further argues that Plaintiff undertook the risk of “collateral deficiency or collateral investment loss” pursuant to the SLA, and therefore any claims based on collateral investment losses are contractually released. I conclude that in this context “operation” is ambiguous and there is an issue of fact whether “collateral investment loss” includes the risk of Wells Fargo investing collateral in securities that did not meet the criteria set forth in the SLA.
reason: The proposed issue identifies the conflict between the Participant’s assumption of investment losses, the Bank’s assumption of losses from negligent operation, and the SLA’s investment-safety mandate. The court addressed that same allocation conflict by asking whether negligent, noncompliant collateral investments fall within the Bank’s “operation” liability or the Participant’s assumed “collateral investment loss.”

issue: "Negligent and fraudulent operation" is conjunctive as written, so it can be read to require both negligence and fraud before the Bank bears any loss, and "operation of its Securities Lending Program" does not say whether investment of cash collateral is "operation". The mis-typed conjunction changes the scope of the Bank's assumed risk.
court_defect: The court construed the ambiguity in whether “operation” of the Securities Lending Program includes investment of cash collateral. It also considered whether the separate allocation of “collateral investment loss” displaced liability for negligent collateral investments.
evidence: Wells Fargo contends that the negligence standard of the SLA does not apply because it imposes liability on Wells Fargo only with respect to the “operation” of the Securities Lending Program, which does not include the investment of the collateral. It further argues that Plaintiff undertook the risk of “collateral deficiency or collateral investment loss” pursuant to the SLA, and therefore any claims based on collateral investment losses are contractually released. I conclude that in this context “operation” is ambiguous and there is an issue of fact whether “collateral investment loss” includes the risk of Wells Fargo investing collateral in securities that did not meet the criteria set forth in the SLA.
reason: The passage directly addresses the proposed issue’s claim that “operation” may or may not encompass investment of cash collateral. It does not address the separate proposed defect that “negligent and fraudulent” conjunctively requires both negligence and fraud, so alignment is substantial but incomplete.

issue: It directly contradicts the opening sentence of Section 8, which gives the Participant "all risk of loss arising out of ... collateral investment loss", leaving no rule for a collateral investment loss caused by negligent Bank operation. The two sentences of the same section allocate the identical loss to opposite parties.
court_defect: The court construed the overlap between the Bank’s assumption of negligent-operation losses and the Participant’s assumption of collateral-investment losses. It found ambiguity as to whether “operation” includes collateral investing and whether “collateral investment loss” encompasses losses caused by the Bank’s noncompliant investments.
evidence: Wells Fargo contends that the negligence standard of the SLA does not apply because it imposes liability on Wells Fargo only with respect to the “operation” of the Securities Lending Program, which does not include the investment of the collateral. It further argues that Plaintiff undertook the risk of “collateral deficiency or collateral investment loss” pursuant to the SLA, and therefore any claims based on collateral investment losses are contractually released. I conclude that in this context “operation” is ambiguous and there is an issue of fact whether “collateral investment loss” includes the risk of Wells Fargo investing collateral in securities that did not meet the criteria set forth in the SLA.
reason: The proposed issue identifies the same competing allocations: Bank liability for negligent operation versus Participant responsibility for collateral-investment loss when the Bank negligently invests the collateral. The court framed the problem as ambiguity and overlap rather than an outright contradiction, but it directly construed the precise interaction the proposed issue names.

issue: The clause simultaneously says the Subscriber relies "solely" on this Agreement, the Confidential Memorandum and "any additional documents furnished or made available by the Trustee," an open-ended category that makes the scope of the non-reliance disclaimer indeterminate.
court_defect: The court construed the disclaimer’s scope and concluded that it did not bar claims based on representations in documents furnished by Wells Fargo or on post-agreement statements. It did not characterize the category of furnished documents as indeterminate.
evidence: However, as noted by Plaintiff, the disclaimer refers to representations made in the Subscription Agreement, the Confidential Memorandum, and any other documents furnished by Wells Fargo. Since the claims are based in part on representations made in documents furnished by Wells Fargo, as well as statements made after the Subscription Agreement was signed in April 2006, the Subscription Agreement does not bar the claims.
reason: Both the proposed issue and the court address the reach of the phrase covering additional or other furnished documents. But the proposed issue alleges ambiguity from that category’s open-endedness, whereas the court applies the category to preserve claims without finding its scope indeterminate.

issue: The operative guarantee reads "not to exceed N/A Dollars ($ N/A)" — the number that makes the guarantee mean anything is absent, so the sentence that follows (costs exceeding the GMP are borne by the Contractor) has no content. That is a writing error that changes what the provision does.
court_defect: The court construed the meaning of “N/A” entered in the guaranteed-maximum-price space—whether it meant “not applicable” or “not available”—and whether the contract therefore had no maximum price or instead an adjustable guaranteed maximum.
evidence: The same article of the contract provides space for a “guaranteed maximum price,” but the parties filled in that space with the term “N/A.” (Id. § 5.2.) The parties dispute what “N/A” means; Metzler says that it means “not applicable” whereas the Ste-phenses say that it means “not available.” (Final Award at 6.)
reason: The proposed issue and the passage focus on the same entry—“N/A” in place of a numerical guaranteed maximum—and both concern whether that leaves the contract without an operative maximum price. Alignment is not exact because the proposal characterizes this as a mechanical omission, while the court treated “N/A” as semantically ambiguous and construed it with other contract provisions.

issue: The Preliminary Budget is defined only as the Contractor's "current best estimate of the Contract Sum, based on industry-standard figures and the Preliminary Drawings," and the clause never says whether the estimate binds the Contractor on price. "Industry-standard figures" is itself an undefined benchmark.
court_defect: The court addressed whether the Preliminary Budget and later Schedule-of-Values adjustments made the agreement a cost-plus-fee contract with an adjustable guaranteed maximum, rather than supporting a competing contractual interpretation. It found that these provisions plausibly created ambiguity about the contract’s price structure.
evidence:
The same section of the contract further provides that as the “Schedule of Values is refined ... a Change Order shall be issued to adjust the Contract Sum.... ” (First Add. § 6.5.) These provisions, as the Ste-phenses argued to the arbitrator, could represent a different type of contract: a cost-plus-fee contract with a guaranteed maximum, albeit one that was adjustable.
Faced with these competing interpretations of the contract terms, each plausibly inconsistent with the other, the arbitrator plausibly determined that the terms of the contract were ambiguous and so turned to extrinsic evidence to determine the parties’ intent.
reason: The passage substantially addresses the proposed issue’s central question—whether the Preliminary Budget operates as a binding price limit—by considering whether it created an adjustable guaranteed maximum. The alignment is not exact because the court framed the defect through the Budget’s interaction with Change Orders and did not address the separate claim that “industry-standard figures” is undefined.

issue: The guarantee is declared "UNCONDITIONALLY AND IRREVOCABLY" yet is immediately qualified as "subject only to the terms of this Policy (which includes each endorsement hereto)"; what an unconditional guarantee of "full and complete payment" means once the endorsements' conditions and exclusions are layered on is genuinely contestable. The operative promise also depends entirely on "Guaranteed Distributions", a term left to Endorsement No. 1.
court_defect: The court construed the scope of “Holder,” deciding whether it included holders of Uninsured Certificates for third-party-beneficiary purposes. It did not construe the tension between “UNCONDITIONALLY AND IRREVOCABLY” and “subject only to the terms of this Policy,” or uncertainty arising from the definition of “Guaranteed Distributions.”
evidence: However, the word “Holder” clearly refers only to holders of Insured Certificates, who benefit from the Policy, not holders of Uninsured Certificates, such as the ESM Parties, who are nowhere referenced in the contract.
reason: The proposed issue concerns qualifications imposed by policy endorsements and the meaning of “Guaranteed Distributions,” whereas the court addressed which certificate owners qualify as a “Holder.” Although both concern the same guarantee sentence, they involve different words and different alleged defects.

issue: Clause (iv) bars Participation in "any business in which he would be reasonably likely to employ, reveal, or otherwise utilize Trade Secrets" in "any geographical area in which the Company or any of its affiliates conduct business" — "reasonably likely" and the trade-secret trigger have no ascertainable boundary, and "the Executive" is a term the Agreement never defines. "Participate" is then given an open-ended "or otherwise" catch-all after a long enumerated list.
court_defect: The court construed whether the phrase “reasonably likely” in the trade-secret noncompete was impermissibly vague or ambiguous and whether the likelihood of Barnett using Aspect’s trade secrets satisfied that standard.
evidence: At this preliminary stage of the litigation, the Court finds little support for Barnett’s position that the phrase “reasonably likely” as used in the Agreement is vague or ambiguous. Courts and the parties have no trouble understanding and applying the concept of reasonable likelihood.
reason: The proposed issue expressly claims that “reasonably likely” and the trade-secret trigger lack an ascertainable boundary, while the court directly decided whether “reasonably likely” was vague or ambiguous. The score is short of complete alignment because the passage does not address the proposed issue’s separate complaints about the undefined term “the Executive” or the “or otherwise” catch-all.

issue: The structure 'Licensor may develop ... a Web page for the Hard Rock Cafe Restaurants, and other Hard Rock Facilities ... except that Licensee may develop ... a Web page for the Hard Rock Hotel/Casinos or Casinos in the Morton Territories' does not say whether Licensee's right is exclusive or merely permissive. It is also unclear whether 'in the Morton Territories' limits the facilities covered or the reach of the web page itself.
court_defect: The court construed whether the “except” clause limited HRCI and granted the Hard Rock Defendants an exclusive right to register a domain name for a casino in the Morton Territories. It also separately construed whether singular “Web page” meant one page total or one page per property.
evidence: The use of the word “except” limits HRCI’s ability to develop, maintain and update websites for Hotel/Casinos and Casinos in the Morton Territories. Additionally, the language “developing], maintaining], and updating] a Web page” is reasonably capable of encompassing the Hard Rock Defendants’ right to register this domain name. The Agreement is therefore ambiguous as to whether it granted the Hard Rock Defendants an exclusive right to register hardrockcasinoalbuquerque.com.
reason: The proposed issue’s exclusivity-versus-permissiveness concern directly matches the court’s finding of ambiguity over whether the provision granted an “exclusive right.” The court did not, however, address the proposed issue’s separate question whether “in the Morton Territories” limits the covered facilities or the geographic reach of the web page.

clause_name: Section 8(b) — Links to Other Party’s Web Pages
issue: 'Both parties agree to include links to the other party's Web pages' specifies no placement, prominence, number or duration, so what performance satisfies the promise is indeterminate. A dispute would turn entirely on filling that gap.
court_defect: The court found “other party’s Web pages” undefined and ambiguous as to whether it includes pages for sublicensed properties. It also treated omission of the Tulsa and Albuquerque properties from pull-down lists as a failure to provide required links.
evidence:
However, by omitting the Tulsa and Albuquerque Properties from its pull down lists, HRCI failed to link to those properties on its web site.
HRCI also asserts that it does not have to link to properties that are sub-licensed by the Hard Rock Defendants. However, the term “other party’s Web pages” is not defined. It could be interpreted to refer to properties that the Hard Rock Defendants sublicensed. The title of section eight, “Joint Cooperation,” lends support to such an interpretation. Because paragraph 8(b) is ambiguous, HRCI’s motion to dismiss this counterclaim for breach of contract is also denied.
reason: The proposed issue includes the absence of a specified number or scope of required links, and the court addressed that component by deciding whether particular properties—and potentially sublicensed properties—had to be linked. The court did not engage with the proposed concerns about prominence, duration, or placement as such, so the overlap is substantial but partial.

issue: 'Any or all of the rights and licenses granted hereunder' is unqualified — no consent, no standards for sublicensees, no limit on the number or duration. Whether it permits a transfer of the entire licence in substance is contestable.
court_defect: The court construed whether Section 10 authorized the Hard Rock Defendants to sublicense or franchise trademark-use rights for the Tulsa and Albuquerque properties. It held that “any or all” of the granted rights included the right to use the Hard Rock Marks in operating those properties.
evidence: HRCI also argues that arbitration is not proper because the use of the Hard Rock Marks at the Tulsa and Albuquerque Properties is not authorized by the Agreement. (PI. Opp’n at 21.) However, the Agreement indicates that the Hard Rock Defendants “have the right to sublicense or franchise any or all of the rights and licenses granted [in the Agreement].” (Agreement ¶ 10.) This includes the right to use the Hard Rock Marks “in connection with or relating to the operation of the Hard Rock Hotel/Casinos or Hard Rock Casinos.” (Agreement ¶ 1(1); see also Agreement ¶¶ 2(a), 4(a).)
reason: Both concern the breadth of “any or all of the rights and licenses,” and the court applied that language to authorize sublicensed trademark use. But the court did not address whether sublicensing all rights amounts to a transfer of the entire license, nor the absence of consent, standards, numerical limits, or duration limits, so the specific alleged defect differs.

issue: 'Any and all services provided by Licensee in connection with or relating to the operation of the Hard Rock Hotel/Casinos' is boundless at the edges: whether entertainment events, broadcasts or third-party concessions are 'Licensed Services' is genuinely arguable. The definition drives the quality obligations in Section 4(a) and 4(d), so its reach matters.
court_defect: The court construed whether the broad definition of “Licensed Services” encompassed the Rehab television program, which HRCI characterized as an unauthorized entertainment product, so that claims about its quality were arbitrable.
evidence: HRCI also asserts that Rehab is an unauthorized “entertainment product” and beyond the scope of the Arbitration Clause. (PI. Opp’n at 22.) However, the Agreement permits the Hard Rock Defendants to use the Hard Rock Marks “in connection with the ... promotion of Hard Rock Hotel/Casinos and Hard Rock Casinos.” (Agreement ¶ 2(a) (emphasis added); see also ¶ 4(a).) This “promotion, advertising or marketing ... and broadcasting” may be done “anywhere in the world.” (Agreement ¶ 2(a).) Moreover, the Arbitration Clause refers all claims concerning the “nature and quality” of “Licensed Services” to arbitration. (Agreement ¶ 4(a).) “Licensed Services” is defined broadly to include “any and all services provided by [the Hard Rock Defendants] in connection with or relating to the operation of [the Hotel].” (Agreement ¶ 1(1) (emphasis added).) Because Rehab portrays a party at the Hotel, it relates to the Hotel’s services. Rehab is also clearly promotional in that it advertises the Hotel to Rehab’s television audience.
reason: The proposed issue identifies uncertainty over whether entertainment and broadcasts fall within the expansive “in connection with or relating to” definition. The court addressed that precise scope question and held that the Rehab entertainment program was related to and promotional of the Hotel; the score is slightly below exact because the proposed issue also gestures toward other edge cases, such as third-party concessions, that the passage does not address.

issue: The worldwide carve-out — Licensee may 'engage in the promotion, advertising or marketing (not including the sale of merchandise) and broadcasting of the Hard Rock Hotel/Casinos ... anywhere in the world' — has no boundary: whether a televised programme or other content is 'promotion ... and broadcasting of' the licensed facilities, as against unlicensed extraterritorial use of the Marks, is squarely contestable. 'Solely in connection with ... promotion of' in the grant sentence carries the same uncertainty.
court_defect: The court construed the scope of the term “exclusive license,” specifically whether it barred HRCI from opening other Hard Rock-branded ventures in the Morton Territories. It concluded that the Agreement barred only specified Hotel/Casino development, not restaurants or music venues.
evidence:
Moreover, use of the term “exclusive license” does not create ambiguity. In the Agreement, “exclusive license” means that HRCI may not license the Hard Rock Marks to others, or compete with the Hard Rock Defendants’ right to use the Hard Rock Marks in the Morton Territories.
The Hard Rock Defendants argue that the term “exclusive license” means HRCI cannot compete with the Hard Rock Defendants “with respect to the particular products or particular territories for which the exclusive license was granted.” (Defs’ Opp’n at 5.).
