But no provision in the Agreement prohibits HRCI from opening other Hard Rock branded ventures such as restaurants and music venues in the Morton Territories. The Agreement only forbids HRCI from developing Hotel/Casinos in the Morton territories and Hotels in Nevada. (See Agreement ¶ 3(a).)
reason: The proposed issue concerns the boundary of the worldwide promotion-and-broadcasting carve-out and the phrase “solely in connection with ... promotion of.” The court instead construed “exclusive license” and what competition by HRCI it prohibited; although it discussed Section 2(a)’s territorial scope generally, it did not engage with the worldwide carve-out or the distinction between promotional broadcasting and unlicensed extraterritorial use.

issue: 'All rights not specifically granted' turns on how 'specifically granted' is read, and the grant in Section 2(a) is expressed in broad functional language ('use and exploit ... in connection with the development, operation ... and promotion'). The reservation therefore has no determinate residue.
court_defect: The court construed whether the scope of the Section 2(a) license, together with Section 3(a)’s reservation of ungranted rights, was ambiguous and whether HRCI retained rights to other Hard Rock-branded ventures in the licensed territories. It held that the grant was narrow, the provisions were unambiguous, and rights outside the specified hotel/casino uses remained with HRCI.
evidence: The Hard Rock Defendants’ exclusive license is narrow: they may use the Hard Rock Marks “only” in the Morton Territories and “solely” in connection with the operations of Hard Rock Hotel Casinos and Hard Rock Casinos. (Agreement ¶ 2(a).) That license is narrowed further by several restrictions on the use of the Hard Rock Marks (see, e.g., Agreement ¶¶ 2(b)(i)-(ix)) and a clause reserving “[a]ll rights not specifically granted to [the Hard Rock Defendants]” to HRCI (Agreement ¶ 3(a)). None of these provisions are ambiguous.
reason: The proposed issue claims that the breadth of Section 2(a)’s functional grant makes the residue under “all rights not specifically granted” indeterminate. The court directly considered the grant together with that reservation, characterized the grant as narrow, and expressly rejected ambiguity, so it engaged with substantially the same alleged defect even though it did not separately parse the words “specifically granted.”

issue: The sentence first preserves Licensor's rights only 'outside the Morton Territories' and then gives Licensor the Hotel Marks 'anywhere in the world for a Hotel facility that does not include a Casino' — the second limb is on its face wider than the first. The Nevada carve-out implies the wider reading, but the clause does not say so.
court_defect: The court construed whether Section 3(a), together with the “exclusive license,” barred HRCI from all competing Hard Rock-branded ventures in the Morton Territories or only from Hotel/Casinos there and Hotels in Nevada. It held that the narrower restrictions applied and that the provisions were unambiguous.
evidence: But no provision in the Agreement prohibits HRCI from opening other Hard Rock branded ventures such as restaurants and music venues in the Morton Territories. The Agreement only forbids HRCI from developing Hotel/Casinos in the Morton territories and Hotels in Nevada. (See Agreement ¶ 3(a).)
reason: The proposed issue concerns whether Section 3(a)’s second limb permits broader worldwide use, including within the Morton Territories, subject to the Nevada exception. The court reached the corresponding territorial construction—only Hotel/Casinos are forbidden in the Morton Territories, while Hotels are forbidden in Nevada—but framed the dispute through the scope of the exclusive license rather than expressly addressing the alleged tension between the sentence’s two limbs.

issue: The standard — 'good quality at least as high as the quality of similar goods presently sold or distributed by Licensee ... at the Las Vegas Hard Rock Hotel/Casino' — benchmarks quality against an unrecorded 1996 snapshot, and 'quality' of services is not defined to say whether it reaches content, image or tone as opposed to workmanship. Both limbs invite competing readings.
court_defect: The court construed whether “quality” is limited to production values or degree of excellence, or instead also encompasses a program’s content and the character, range, and experience of hotel services.
evidence: HRCI argues that the dispute concerning Rehab involves its “content” and not its quality. Quality, according to HRCI, is “the show’s production values[,] cinematography,” (PI. Opp’n at 22), or “acting in the program” (Hr’g Tr. dated Feb. 15, 2011 (“Tr.”) at 22). Defendant further argues that although the forum-selection clause and the Service of Suit Endorsement do not conflict, to the extent they do, the forum-selection clause controls because it was not changed or modified by the Service of Suit Endorsement. Thus, the Court must determine whether, when interpreted within the contract as a whole, the two provisions conflict and create an ambiguity.
As discussed above, the forum selection clause provides for New York as the designated forum, whereas the Service of Suit Endorsement unambiguously permits Plaintiff, as the policy holder, to choose the forum to bring suit. Thus, when read separately and in isolation, the two provisions appear to conflict.

clause_name: Service of Suit Endorsement — Reservation of Rights

evidence:
On the same page and immediately following the Service of Suit provision discussed above, the Endorsement further states: “All other terms and conditions of this Policy remain unchanged.” By specifying that “other terms and conditions ... remain unchanged,” the Endorsement further demonstrates that the terms and conditions listed directly above — including “we, at your request will submit to the jurisdiction of a court of competent jurisdiction within the United States” — in fact changed the original insurance agreement. Thus, the plain language of the Service of Suit Endorsement unambiguously states in two separate places — both before and after the provision providing that Defendant will “submit” to the forum of Plaintiffs choosing — that the Endorsement changes the Policy to correspond with the Endorsement’s provisions.
Accordingly, the Court finds that upon interpreting the Policy as a whole, the Service of Suit Endorsement modified the forum selection clause so that the plain language of the Policy unambiguously permits Plaintiff to bring suit in a forum of its choosing.
reason: The proposed issue identifies uncertainty over whether the unchanged-terms sentence leaves the New York forum clause operative alongside the Service of Suit provision. The court addressed that exact conflict and priority question, although it resolved the issue by holding that the endorsement modified the forum-selection clause rather than leaving priority unresolved.

issue: The 11% rate applies to "Net Sales of all Albums sold by PRI for distribution through Normal Retail Channels in the United States"; whether a given exploitation (in particular new digital configurations) is an Album "sold" through "Normal Retail Channels" or is instead a licensed use is genuinely open on these words. The fit is not perfect because the proposal characterizes § 7.06 broadly as covering licences and posits simultaneous classification, while the court focuses specifically on § 7.06(a)(ii)’s enumerated distribution methods.

clause_name: Section 7.06(a) — Fifty-percent royalty for specified exploitation

clause_name: Section 7.06(a) — Fifty-percent royalty for specified exploitation
issue: This paragraph cannot be reconciled with paragraph 7.02(a), which pays 11% of the Royalty Base for Albums sold through Normal Retail Channels; one and the same exploitation can be described as a licence under 7.06(a) and a sale under 7.02(a), and no provision states which prevails. But the proposed issue alleges an unresolved overlap between licensed and retail sales, whereas the court addressed the scope of “or other methods” and found that digital downloads were not covered by § 7.06(a)(ii), without construing a no-priority conflict with § 7.02(a).

issue: "Claim" turns on "a written demand against any Insured for monetary or non-monetary relief", an undefined phrase whose application to letters, charges and pre-suit correspondence is the classic claims-made battleground; the paragraph also speaks of an Insured "receiv[ing]" a civil proceeding. When a Claim was first made is the pivotal issue under this policy.

It also determined from that construction when the claim was made.
evidence:
Alternatively, FINRA contends that “the phrase ‘written demand’ is ambiguous” and the Court must construe it “in favor of the insured, FINRA.” Pl.’s Mem. 17. It is true that in Maryland, courts construe ambiguous language in insurance contracts “against the insurer as the drafter of the instrument,’ ” if they cannot ascertain the meaning through extrinsic or parol evidence. Sullins v. Allstate Ins. Co., 340 Md. 503, 667 A.2d 617, 619 (1995) (quoting Cheney v. Bell Nat’l Life, 315 Md. 761, 556 A.2d 1135, 1140 (1989)). However, as discussed, the language at- issue simply is not ambiguous.
For all these reasons, I conclude, as a matter of law, that the February 3, 2011 email is a “claim” as the term is used in the Policies. See Bd. of Educ. of Charles Cnty., 569 A.2d at 1296. Further, the material facts are undisputed: The email is from February 3, 2011, and the 2011/2012 Policy provided coverage for claims made between March 31, 2011 and March 31, 2012. Therefore, the claim was not made during the period covered by the 2011/2012 Policy.
reason: The proposed issue identifies uncertainty over whether pre-suit correspondence constitutes a “written demand” and consequently when the claim was first made; the court expressly resolved both questions. The proposed issue’s separate observation about an Insured “receiv[ing]” a civil proceeding was not addressed, preventing complete alignment.

issue: "A written demand against any Insured for monetary or non-monetary relief" is the classic contested trigger: whether a letter, a charge, or a request for corrective action is such a demand is open. The reach of "similar formal proceeding before another federal, state or other governmental agency" is a further general-catch-all boundary.
court_defect: The court construed whether an email stating a specific settlement amount qualified as a “written demand against any Insured for monetary or non-monetary relief,” despite reiterating an earlier oral communication and allegedly lacking formalities. It held that the language was unambiguous and that the email was a claim.
evidence: Although Plaintiff argues that the email is not a demand, the term “demand” in the Policies certainly encompasses the circumstances presented in the email. Neither this Court nor the Maryland appellate courts have construed “demand” in the artificially restricted context urged by Plaintiff; Accordingly, I will consider the case law in other districts. In construing the same language, albeit ordered differently (“a written demand for monetary or nonmonetary relief made against any Insured”), the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois stated that “demand for ‘relief is a broad enough term to include a demand for something due.” Minuteman Int’l, Inc. v. Great Am. Ins. Co., No. 03 C 6067, 2004 WL 603482, at *3 & *7 (N.D.Ill. Mar. 22, 2004); see Agilis Ben. Servs. LLC v. Travelers Cas. & Sur. Co. of Am., No. 5:08-CV-213, 2010 WL 8573372, at *6 (E.D.Tex. Apr. 30, 2010) (same). Here, Reich’s counsel stated in the email that, in his prior conversation with FINRA’s general counsel, he “said that Mr. Reich believed that FIN-RA’s decision to terminate his employment was discriminatory” and “added that Mr. Reich would settle that claim for a sum equal to 5 years’ pay.” Feb. 3, 2011 email. It is clear that Reich, through counsel, was asserting a legal claim for employment discrimination and demanding money in an amount equal to his salary for five years to settle that claim. See id. Any other reading of the email is fanciful. The email is a demand not for an amorphous “something due” but specifically for a monetary payment of a specifically requested amount. Cf. Minuteman, 2004 WL 603482, at *7. It is of no moment that the email clarifies a prior oral demand, as it still states the demand, and it manifests the demand in written format.
reason: The proposed issue’s principal defect—uncertainty over what communications constitute a “written demand” for relief—is exactly what the court construed when deciding whether the email qualified. The passage does not address the separate catch-all boundary for a “similar formal proceeding,” so alignment is strong but not complete.

clause_name: Section 14.1 — Just-cause termination and cessation of obligations

issue: "Unmodified derivatives" (alongside "progeny", "portions" and "any accompanying know-how or data") is the pivotal ambiguous term: it is undefined and leaves open whether a new lentiviral construct built from the transferred construct is itself "Material". The catch-all "any accompanying know-how or data" adds a further boundary problem against the enumerated physical items.
court_defect: The court construed whether the definition of “Material,” particularly its inclusion of “unmodified derivatives” and “portions,” encompassed the newly created June lentiviral construct or excluded it as a modified derivative. It concluded that the parties’ competing interpretations of the definition’s scope were reasonable, making the provision facially ambiguous.
evidence: Penn suggests, without concluding, that the contract is ambiguous, see Penn Resp. in Opp. at 15-16, and it offers an alternative interpretation of the contract language. According to Penn, the phrase “progeny, portions, unmodified derivatives and any accompanying know-how or data” does not encompass the June Construct because the June Construct is a “modified derivative,” or “a substance created from all or part of another, but ... requir[ing] a change relative to the original substance during the creation process”, Penn Resp. in Opp. at 16. Penn contrasts this with an unmodified derivative, which the agreement specifically includes and which Penn describes as “a substance that can be formed directly from another without a change to the original substance”. Id. Penn argues that the contract’s definition of materials “does not broadly encompass any and all derivatives of the biological materials provided”, but instead “specifies very limited types of derivatives of the biological materials to be included”, of which “modified derivatives” is not one. Id.

Reading modified derivatives as excluded from the MTA is also appropriate, Penn contends, in light of paragraph three of the 2007 MTA where Penn agreed that “the Materials are provided for the sole purpose of allowing [Penn] to use Materials to produce a molecular lentiviral vector clone incorporating Materials ... for application in ex vivo autologous cell modification .... ” 2007 MTA ¶ 3; Penn Resp. in Opp. at 17 (emphasis added). This passage does not refer to the lentiviral clone as itself a “material”, and the commercialization constraints in the 2003 MTA and 2007 MTA do not refer to products “incorporating Materials”, but those “con-tainting] materials” (2003 MTA) or “containing] a portion of the Materials, ... derived from the Materials, or which could not have been produced but for the use of the Materials.” (2007 MTA). Penn argues that the June Construct does not contain a “portion” of the materials because it does not contain “a physical part of the whole provided by St. Jude”, Penn Resp. in Opp. at 20, but instead contains a modified derivative.
Penn also points to paragraph five of the 2007 MTA which provides that with regard to patents “[o]wnership shall follow inventorship according to U.S. patent law.” Penn reads this as demonstrating a “clear intent ... to allow the University to research and create a new substance in which it would presumably have its own rights”, while under St. Jude’s interpretation, “even a copy of a single nucleotide, molecule, or even atom from the Campana Construct would constitute a ‘portion’ of the Materials”, Penn Resp. in Opp. at 20-21.
St. Jude and Penn reach contrary conclusions about the scope of the definition of “materials”, and we find that both are reasonable. The contract is thus facially ambiguous.
